(Continued.) 7- Each Island constitutes a separate elective District The Judges in the three Towns and in St. Johns, each in their Jurisdiction have to conduct the elections as Directors. The Burgher Council respectively prepares yearly a list of all those entitled to vote in the elective District, and another list of those who are eligible, with a com-

plete statement of their names alphabetically. vocation and abode. When the lists arc completed they are to be exhibited in a proper place for 14 days, notice to that effect to be given previously. 8. If any person is found in the list who is not qualified to vote, or any person wrongly omitted, any one may in writing state the fact to the Director in the J urisdiction where the concerned lives, and produce proofs within 3 days from the expiration of the time ia which the lists are exhibited for inspection. The objections or remarks thus made against the lists, are to he decided upon by the electoral Committee, consisting of the Director, a member of the Burgher Council, and another trustworthy person appointed by the Burgher Council for that purpose, in a public meeting to be kept in the course of the following 8 days. The persons who have made the representation or remarks, as well as those regarding whom such representations have been made, are to be summoned to this meeting, where the last mentioned will receive a copy of the writing containing the representation relative to them Should the decision in any way affect the eligibility of a person the necessary publication in this respect must be made in a proper manner

9. The day for the public election will be fixed by the directors respectively. In St. Croix the election ought to take place on the same day in both Jurisdictions, and the electors may vote on any eligible citizen without regard to whether he lives in the one or the other Jurisdiction. The electoral Directors must at least 4 days previous to the election, in the usual manner, publish in what place the meeting is to be kept, and likewise the day and the hour when it is to commence and when it is to be closed, furthermore the names are to be given of the retiring members and of the substitute members.

10 The electoral Committee meets at the election the day and hour appoiutcd, and brings with him the list for the whole elective district, with the additional corrections, as iiir as such have taken place according to 8. The Director opens the election, and provides for the elections proceeding in the best order possible. Every person desirous of exercising his right of voting must appear personally at the place of election. When giving his votes, he mentions as many persons a? are to be elected in his district, (see 6) stating at the same time their names, rank and vocation The votes to be registered in two Protocols, one in charge of each of the Director's assistants, the one to contain the name of each voter, and alongside of it the names of the persons he elects, and in the other the names of the elected and under each of them the names of the voters. The minutes to be read to the voter, verified by him and compared together. When no more persons request to take part in the voting, (election) the members of the electoral Committee will then add their own votes The voting being finished, the votes of each of the elected arc to bfi summed up, and in St Croix the two electoral Committees to give mutual notice of the result of the elections, the persons who have attained the greatest number of votos are then declared to be Members of the Burgher Council, and the two who after the laatmentioned have the highest number of votes, become substitute members. If two or more

persons have an equal number of votes, then the result to be decided by drawing of lots by the foreman 11. Those who have been elected will receive written notice regarding their election from the Director, who at the same time has to report the result of the Election to the superior authority. In case the person elected states an excuse, the Burgher Council will have to decide whether the same can be considered sufficient Any person having obtained the age of 60 years or who in the last 3 years has been member of tho Burgher Council and officiated as such for at least 3 years, can decline to accept the election. The same is applicablo to all Employe# (functionaries. ) The Governor, and the Government's Secretary, the Commandant of St. Thotua# and tho Scorctary, are according to their position not eligible. TIIE COLONIAL GARRISONS. Few of the English papers have drawn public attention to the remarkable fact, that while wo are arming in the East wc are disarming in the West, or that while we are sending a fleet into the Black Sea we are removing the þÿQueen s troops, for the first time in our history, from our Colonics, and leaving the unfortunate colonists to protect themselves in the best way they can. One of the favourite cries of Cobden, Bright, and generally of the whole Manchester School of free-booters and destructives, has long been þÿ no colonies and one of the base methods of most easily gettiug rid of those magnificent appendages upon which they have laid the most stress, has been the cry of removing the colonial garrisons on grounds of pretended economy, and letting the Colonists shift for themselves. Cobden, in the peace Conference, at Edinburgh, iu October last, after enlarging on the cost to the nation of army and navy, threatened something like a motion of his own in the House of Commons for a þÿ radical colonial þÿreform in military expenditure. The last packet from the West Indies shows that our , ingenious Ministry of All the Talents, who eared to harrow all their policy from the þÿdog s seem book of the Free trade and þÿl eacc Conference agitator, aud to be incapable of raising their views beyond the low level of that, the shallowest of all doctrinaire parties, have been beforehand with the frothy member of the west riding, and have actually iu good earnest, at the moment when ex- are on the eve of war, commenced the very we

periment in our colonies of withdrawing that troops from them so recklessly advocated by our mischievous leader of a miserable faction. The despatch addressed by the Duke of Newcastle to Sir William Colebrooke, Governor General of Barbadoes and the Windward Islands, announcing the intention of Government to Gre- move the whole of the þÿQueen troops s from renada, St. Vincent and Tobago, and to dismantle the garrisons of those loyal and well affected islands, has spread the greatest consternation throughout every part of the group of the West Indian colonies where it has been made known, because it is considered, and of course justly, that though the orders of the Ministry have immediate reference only to the three islands / named, it is the first blow struck of a new and most dangerous premeditated attack by the Imperial Government against the whole of the British Colonics, no matter whore situated, whether in the Caribbean Sea, on the North American Continent, or in the Southern hemisphere. It is in short, the insidious, almost, traitorous, assertion of a principle of colonial policy quite unparalleled in British annals, and most alarming to all true friends of this great and glorious empire, no mat-

ter whether they be personally connected with our colonies or not þÿ whether regard be had to its unconstitutional nature, or the critical time chosen for its promulgation. tion Forbearing in Parliament as the great Conservative opposi- have shown themselves towards the present Coalition Cabinet, of which forbearance towards political opponents is certainly no eharacteristic quality, and assailable as, unfortunately, the measures of the Cabinet on too many weak points, it is still to be earnestly hoped for the good of the empire, that an opportunity will be embraced in the approaching session by the friends of constitutional government to take the sense of Parliament on the inauguration of of this new unheard of monstrous, dismembering scheme of Ministerial colonial policy. It is true that the Duke of þÿNewcastle s despatch to Sir Wm. Colebrooke, says, I am in þÿ communication with the Board of Admiralty upon the subject of placing a vessel of war at your dis- þÿ þÿposal. vessel of þÿwar Why, what is the good of placing at Sir William þÿColebrooke þÿ s com- a þÿmand, when the garrisons are withdrawn from these islands ? Of what use would a frigate be, cruising about in the neighbourhood in the event of an insurrection breaking out in any one of those islands, the buildings of the estates being burnt, the towns sacked, or the throats of the peaceable and orderly inhabitants cutþÿ events which we sincerely implore may not take place, but which the Duke of Newcastle aud the rest of

her þÿMajesty s present advisers have done their best to bring about ? A ship of war might be of some use in chastising and taking revenge for disturbances of the public peace, after they had broken out, aud the mischief had been done ; but it is clear that under no circumstances could the blue-jackets or the marines prevent riots in the bosom of any country þÿ still less where, as in this case, one vessel would be expected to do the duty of beadle for three islands, none lying at a nearer distance to any one of the others than a þÿday s sail with a fair wind. The peace Conference howlers may affect to believe that society can be held together without an army or navy ; but those who are more honest, or more observant, and specially such as are acquainted with the present state of the West Indies, will admit, that, with the withdrawal of the regular troops from those countries þÿ all the security for the preservation of life and property must cease. Garrisoned as they have hitherto been by gallant British regiments of the line þÿ it may rarely þÿ indeed have been necessary to call out the troops in aid of the civil power ; still the knowledge possessed by the population that the military were, always on the spot, ready to suppress outrage þÿ has done more to check infractions of social order than all the orders in council and all the despatches of Colonial Secretaries of State from the hour of emancipation to the present. IIow far it may be constitutional or otherwise in the Ministers of the

Crown thus to leave any of our colonics defenceless þÿ and to surrender the Royal garrisons to 1 local þÿauthorities, or failing that to pull the fortification to pieces and sell the materials as old lumber wc leave others to decide. But wc may remark that the shameful threat of tile shameless Cabinet of the northern earl to remove the whole of the forces from those three ill-starred colonics þÿ to ship away the þÿ þÿordnance, to dismantle and sell the þÿ þÿbarracks, and not even to give the þÿ unprotected inhabitants the benefit of the small þÿarms, unless they buy them þÿ is the more unjustifiable when we consider that before it was decided upon to proceed to these extremities no fair opportunity whatever was afforded the inhabitants of taking any measures, however hasty and insufficient, for their own safety. It may be asked why, of all the colonies in the West Indies, St. Vincent, Grenada, and Tobago should have been chosen as the first victims of this perilous experiment ? We fear the answer must be, that St. Vincent, Grenada and Tobago, have been thus punished because they are loyal þÿ because they have the misfortune to be favourably known at the Colonial Office as quiet and peaceable islands, which have rarely given any trouble to the chiefs or the rising young statesmen of that department of the public service. There is little doubt that such is the true explanation of the odious pre-eminence thus thrust on those three well conducted dependencies. There is too much reason to fear, that what was

well said of the late Sir Robert Peel that he conceded everything to clamour and inflicted everything on loyalty, may, with even more truth and very considerable augmentations, be said of our present rulers. The question, however, is one which must soon procure for itself the consideration of Parliament. þÿ Morning Herald

From the Bath Chronicle, April 6, 1854. We agree with Lord Derby that there would have been no Russian war if the Karl of Aberdeen had not, by chance, become Prime Minister of England. The truth of this appears as palpable as the most glorious or the most disgraceful fact in our national history. Lord Aberdeen has always considered Turkey "a dying man and his policy has tended to hasten the catastrophe. It is his boast that he made Greece an independent state, in preference to placing it under the sovereignty of the Sultan, believing that the Ottoman empire was about to pass away. He gave Russia permission, in 1829, to blockade the Turkish ports in the Mediterranean. He trained the treaty on which her present demands are based. In J 842, when Russia was intriguing to effect in Servia what she has accomplished in Wallachia, Lord Aberdeen declared that she had a right to ut her own construction on her own treaties þÿ ad a right, in other words, to do that to resist which England has now plunged into war. In 1844, when the Emperor of Russia visited thi3 country for the express purpose, as it turns out, of securing the partition of Turkey, Lord Aberdeen held personal and secret conferences with him, and entered into an agreement which has ever since been the base of his operations. The object of that document, according to Lord Derby, was to partition Turkey between Russia, Austria, and England. France was to be isolated, and thus excluded from a share of the spoil. Lord Aberdeen, however, represents the agreement as

a very harmless thing þÿ meaning little, pledging the country to nothing. It is, he says, a mere engagement that nothing shall be done in settling the affairs of Turkey, should she become defunct, without previous concert between England and Russia. Rut if this were really all it means, why so much mystery ? Why was it made the subject and his friend þÿ of a personal conference between the Emperor " between gentlemen," not between ministers of state acting officially ? Why did Lord Aberbecn withhold the agreement from his colleagues ? Lord Derby who was colonial minister at the time distinctly states that it was never brought under the notice of the Cabinet. Why did Lord Aberdeen prevent any copy of it being made, and exclude any intimation of its existence from the archives of the state ? Why, when Lord Clarendon inserted a short passage from it, in a despatch to the British Ambassador in St. Petersburg, did the Emperor protest against any reference to it, as a breach of confidence, insisting that it should not be inserted in that despatch when laid before Parliament ? Why was the agreement kept close locked in a box and handed mysteriously from Lord Aberdeen to his successor Lord Pahnerston ; and to his successor Lord Granville ; and to his successor Lord Malmcsbury ; and to his successor Lord Clarendon ? Whv was it concealed from our Ambassador at St. Petersburg, if there was nothing in it to be concealed ? W hy did the Russian Ambassador dog every newly appointed minister into the Fo-

reign Office to tell him of this agreement, if it were a mere generality r There can be no reason for þÿmystery every reason for publicity þÿ if the agreement really contains "nothing but that which is wise Sp moderate and judicious" þÿ nothing whatever to which he is not ready to subscribe at this moment as Lord Aberdeen says in that insolent þÿ tone which ho has assumed with the Premiership. Lord Aberdeen, however, can only consider the document unimportant at the sacrifice of his political sagacity. He ought to have been warned by the pains taken to obtain it, to conceal its existence, give to it a good appearance, that there was something more in it than met the eye. He might have reasonably suspected that it was the beginning of an end ; and that end is transparent The designs of Russia upon Turkey, as we are told by Lord ralmerston, are not of yesterday, nor have they grown up with the present generation. The possession of Turkey has been the ambition of Russia, from the days of Peter the have derived their surprising, their ideas of govern- Great ; nor is it religion, since the Russians ment, and even their vices, from the Byzantine empire, which some people now hope to see revived. The march of Russia upon Europe lies ; ceivcd. He measured them through Constantinople. Russia, it has been well said, without a port is like a vigorous man choking from the want of external air ; it is like a giant cramped by want qf room to move bis limbs. The possession of the Dardanelles would give her

that access to the world beyond her frontiers which P Peter the Great did not secure by ctersburjgh , nor his successor by seizing the erecting St. Crimea, situated as they are on the edgo of frozen seas Until Russia obtains an outlet which is not frozen up during eight months of the year, the Russian navy will be a plaything, again and again

AT i destroyed in its icy prison. To burst these bars is, then, the grand aim of Russian policy. All other things are made to gravitate towards that end. The course of other nations is deflected by intrigue or violence to serve it. Delay has only shurpcncd the desire ; but with that impassibility, in which, in our own century, a sovereign has been murdered without hate, and his son even now tolerates his father's murderers, there is no hurry þÿ no eager grasping at the prize, no shaking of the tree before the ripening of the pear. Lord Aberdeen knows, or ought to have known, that the eye of Russia has ever been fixed on her prey, and, therefore, be ought not to have committed himself to this agreement. He has himself lived to see the partition of Poland ; the armed neutrality of the Baltic, by which Catherine hoped to destroy the maritime power of England ; the treaty between Napoleon and Alexander, by which the latter sought to secure the keys of his house ; the conquest of the Asiatic shores of the Black Sea ; the secret treaty of Unkiar Schelessi, by which that sea was converted into a Russian lake ; and these things should have taught him to beware of casting in the lot of this country with a Russian Emperor. He might more reasonably have concluded that an agreement so anxiously sought, so gravely treated, was not the mere matter of course which he now affects to consider it ; þÿ but a scheme for realizing its malignant prophesies the small end of the wedge intended to rend

that Empire which is the subject of it. The Emperor of Russia himself has always attached the greatest importance to this agreement. Baron Brunow, his ambassador in this country, " the key of all the conferences with Russia" described it to Lord Malmesbury as since it was entered into. The Emperor has made it the foundation, the motive, and the defence, of his policy towards Turkey. It is clear that he considered the partition of Turkey a settled point, whenever its condition created the opportunity. It is clear that he considered Lord Aberdeen pledged to aid and abet him by the word of a gentleman ; and we can now understand why he has so continually harped on the personal parole d'honneur, seeing that it is the sheet anchor of his eastern policy. We say again, there would have been no Russian war if there had been no Aberdeen ministry. The Emperor had framed a personal document with a British minister, who shared his views as regards iurkey þÿ aye, who promoted the Russian designs by his official acts. The consummation was delayed by the overthrow of the Peel administration, and the consequent dismissal of a minister whom he has always regarded as an accomplice, and whom Lord John Russell þÿ let into the secret by becoming Foreign Minister þÿ denounced as a Russian conspirator, in his memorable defence of ing Lord Palmerston's manlier foreign policy. Noth- couid lie done while this old friend" this " þÿ minister who he boasted would be brought into his designs by ten minutes' conversation þÿ was

out of office. But no sooner did Lord Aberdeen vault into the Premiership, than the Emperor sent his congratulations, and proceeded to " enforce his bond. The time was come þÿ dy>ng man" must die, now that Lord Aber- the deen was at the head of affairs in England. Lord Aberdeen who thought as he did regarding the present aud future of Turkey who had given þÿ him leave to strain treaties to suit his own interests þÿ who had entered into a secret agreement with him þÿ who had obsequiously concealed its existence from his colleagues, from Parliament and from the public þÿ was now able to work with him. And then commenced the secret correspondence, founded on the agreement. Ho was led to expect connivance or complicity by Lord Aberdeen's engagement; by another cabinet minister's declaration; that the integrity and independence of Turkey were not facts, but phantoms aud phrases. No opposition was to be expected from Lord John Russell, for Lord Aberdeen was supreme ; nor from Lord I'almerston, for he was a discredited minister. The Emperor was further encouraged by the credence which the British government gave to assurances intended to deceive, in spite of facts within their own knowledge, as if they were willing to be deby the standard of his own faithlessness ; he interpreted their protestations and actions, their assurances in favour of peace, and their demonstrations of war alike þÿ by the light of the secret agreement. He was assured even by the meekness of the refusal with

which his proposition was met. lie might reasonably imagino that words had been used to mask thoughts and intentions ; for if England had telt insulted by the offer of Egypt and Candia as her share of tho spoil, she would have usod different language þÿ she would have declined to enter into tho discussion of the fate of Turkey þÿ

she would not have admitted that the interferwas " prescribed by duty and sanctioned by ence of Russia with the internal affairs of Turkey, treaty." Circumstances favoured the Emperor's view of the case. Lord Aberdeen was opposed to the establishment of the French empire, and had censured Lord Derby's government for recognising it. Two of his colleagues had bitterly reviled the Emperor, by necessity a tyrant, though th'ey had not one word of reproach to throw at the old friend of their chief, un hereditary tyrant. The Czar might naturally conclude (Lord Palmerston having been excluded from the Foreign office for applauding the coup de main which made Louis Napoleon Emperor þÿ other ministers having reviled him þÿ the English people having armed themselves against a Bonapartist invasion) that there could be no union between England and France þÿ that France must be isolated and be compelled to consent to the extinction of the Turkish empire, not being able to prevent it. He, therefore, pronounced the doom of Turkey, and when he found that Lord Aberdeen did not second his resolution þÿ that Lord Palmerston and Lord John Russell were lions in the þÿway because the people of England raised their voice in the cause of the oppressed þÿ no wonder he complained that he had been deceived, and retorted the epithet "fraudulent," which Lord John Russell affixed to him, by declaring that the noble lord and his colleagues were parties to the fraud. Lord Aberdeen committed a grave fault in con-

senting to a personal and unofficial correspondence with a foreign Prince, whose ambitious designs were notorious ; in embodying their joint views in a secret agreement which while it has been concealed from the peop'e who were to have been engaged by it, has been held over their rulers as a bond lroui which there was no escape. He acted more as the willing tool of Russia, than as tho Minister of a free country, amenable to the judgment of public opinion. Lord Clarendon says very truly, that all "communications of this kind are exceedingly inconvenient to a constitutional country." Not long since they would have been treasonable. Common sense might have dictated that no conference should have been entered into, certainly no agreement settled, of which it was not safe to keep a copy, even in the secret archives of the nation. Common respect for the national honour might have restrained a discussion of the fate of Turkey after the Emperor of Russia had declared that lie woidd occupy Constantinople if he liked, but that we should not do so under any circumstances, while he had a man or a musket þÿ after he had offered us Egypt and Candia, and thereby betrayed that his aim was the partition of Turkey. Common prudence might have dictated that no reliance was to be placed on his assurances after the avowal of his designs, after his troops were marching to execute them ; and more than one minister was guilty of gross impropriety in assuring Parliament that the Emperor was animated by good faith, when they had proof in

their hands that he was not. The Emperor of Russia has been deceived as well as the people of England. He has been decoyed by his own hopes, by the strange, vacillating policy of Lord Aberdeen, into a position front which there is no safe retreat. But while wc condemn the Earl of Aberdeen, wc do not intend to use his conduct in justification of the Emperor of Russia. We do not defend the Czar to point a thrust at the British Government. If the Emperor has been deceived, he deserves to be deceived. He made a secret compact in one sense, and he expected it to be carried out in another sense. Even if Lord Aberdeen were disposed to go along with him in the construction he has put upon the agreement, the English people would not permit him. Publio opinion has saved Turkey, and, it may be has restrained Lord Aberdeen from facilitating its destruction. The Emperor has tried to steal a march on justice, and has been caught in his own springe. The existence of this agreement, so far from serving his ends, has defeated them ; since it shows that tho attack upon Turkey has not been stimulated by any recent act of the Sultan, as it is pretended, but is an attempt to accomplish the traditional policy of Russia.

From the St. Lucia Palladium , April 15. ANTIGUA. A public meeting was holden in the Court House on Monday last, to devise the best means of carrying into effect an Industrial Exhibition in this Island on the 1st of August next. On the motion of the Venerable the Archdeacon, the Lord Bishop was called to the chair, and on the motion of Mr. Price, Mr. R. S. Heagan was requested to act as Secretary. The following report was then directed to be read. REPORT Of the Sub Committee appointed to prepare a Prospectus of the Industrial Exhibition contemplated in this Island. At a meeting of gentlemen held in the house ofDocof organising an ' Association for the encouragement tor Ledeatt on the 17th December last for the purpose of Industry,' a letter addressed to the Chairman by Mr. Heagan was read, pointing out the importance of stimulating local enterprise, and the formation of habits of Industry amongst all classes of the inhabitants of this and the neighbouring Islands, to make manual labour respectable, and the absence of some regular occupation disreputable, which desirable objects he believed would in some degree be promoted through the medium of an Exhibition or Industrial Bazaar at which specimens of every kind of West Indian product, whether natural or manipulated, would be exposed for examination and sale. A Committee was appointed to confer with Mr. Heagan, to receive further details of his plan, and consider its praticability. This Committee, having had several meetings, decided on the feasibility of the scheme, in presence of evidence of the ex-

istence of a large amount of undeveloped resources in this and the other islands, which would afford remunerative occupation to the industrious poor, resulting in the production of superior articles, not only of a more durable description but at a lower price, than that at present charged on imported articles. The Committee considered that the most certain mode of encouraging local industry would be by the establishment ultimately of a Depot, after the Exhibition, where every species of manufacture and natural product might be exposed collectively for sale ; that ample publicity would thus be given to their existence, and where the prices at which the various descriptions of wares could be furnished might be readily ascertained. Amongst the articles most in demand and which would at all times meet with a ready sale, the following may be enumerated, and for excellence in produ- þÿ Lcdcatt, Esq , M. R. C. P. L. Joseph Shervington, cing which, small prizes should be awarded, v.z: Cabinet work of all kind1, Tortoise shell work, Rope, Cordage, and all kinds of prepared fibrous substances, Lottery every description, Leather, dried and salted of hides, Saddlery and Harness, Boots and Shoes, Baskets and wicker work, Plain and ornamental needle work, Hats of Panama and otljer kinds of straw, and plaited straw, Door, table and other Mats, Bird Cages, Engineering and working models, Machinery, Brass, Copper and Tin work, Whitesmiths' and Blacksmiths' work, Textile fabrics, Paintings and Drawings, Carpenters',

Wheelwrights' and Coopers' work, and all kinds of mechanical work and inventions, Tobacco, Cigars and Snuff, Stuffed and preserved animals, birds, insects and fish, Staple Products, including, Sugar, Rum, unfermenting Molasses, Arrowroot, Tous-les-mois, Potato Flour, Manioc Farine and Tapioca, Cassaripe, Ginger, Cayenne Pepper, Curry Powder, Pickles, all kinds of native Succades, Cotton, Fruits and Vegetables of every kinds, Dried Fish, preserved shell Fish, Honey and bleached Wax, Oils, animal and vegetable, Temper Lime, Native artificial Manure, Fossils, cut and polished, and in the natural state, Shells, &c , Cabinet Wood, Building Materials, & c. &c. &c. But no description of work exhibiting skill or industry, whether useful or ornamental, would be excluded, while a preference would be given to articles of utility, and such as are in daily use. In the production of the above articles much local industry may be beneficially exercised ; besides which many others will suggest themselves to practieal minds. The Committee recommend that an Exhibition embracing as many articles of West Indian industry and skill, and native products, possible, as Bhall be opened in the Court House on the first of August next, and they would suggest that an application be made to the local Legislature for an Act to authorize the introduc tion fkee of duty, of evpry description of articles sent for Exhibition only, but if afterwards sold to be liable to duty, that neighbouring colonies should have every

facility for sending specimens of their skill and natural resources ; and that the Exhibition be kept open for some days, a small fee being charged for admission, such admission fees to be devoted to the establishment of a permanent Depot or Repository for the sale of such wares as it may be desirable to encourage. During the Industrial Exhibition, it is proposed to hold at some convenient place near the Ci y, an Exhibition of native Stock of all descriptions, and to offer prizes for competition. The commhtee propose to invite the co-operation of the whole of the islands in these seas, including the Foreign Islands, in which industry in other objects the ordinary West India staples has reached a high point. The Committee submit the expediency of the day for opening the Exhibition being observed as a general Holiday, and the occasion being marked by such ceremonies as are most fitted to celebrate an effort at advancement in the arts and manufactures, which may, under the Divine blessing, lead to results of vital importance to this and other colonies. Previous to the opening of the Exhibition a Committee should bo appointed to mako arrangements, classify

<0 m ® a x A7J3, articles, and superintend such details of the plan as circumstances may demand. W. M. Ledeatt. C. M. Eldridge. T. Price. R. S. Heagan. Antigua , March , 13 th 1854. The report having been read the following Resolutions were unanimously adopted : þÿ 1st. Moved by the honourable Sir Robert Ilorsford, C. B., seconded by Ilenrv Bourne, Esq. þÿResolved That the Report of the Sub-Committee sanctioned by the general Committee, and now read, be adopted by this meeting, and this meeting pledges itself to use every exertion to carry the projected Exhibition into effect with all possible despatch. 2nd. Communicated. TIIE OLD STRUCTURE AT NEWPORT, RHODE ISLAND Mr. Judah Touro þÿ Prof. Charles C. Rafn þÿ Royal Society Northern Antiquaries. of

The late Mr. Judah Touro, who died a few days since, and whose enormous wealth and exuberant charity find few parallels in the history of humanity in any laud or era, has, in the 21st article of his will, " given and bequeathed to the city of Newport, in the State of Rhode Island, the sum of ten thousand dollars, on condition that the said sum be expended in the said city, known as the " Old Mill," to be kept purchase and improvement of the property in as a public park, promenade ground." The grand historic interest attached to this architectural monument is due, chiefly, to Mr. Charles C. Rafn, Secretary of the Royal Society of Northern Antiquaries, at Copenhagen. During the last summer the learned and much lamented Colonel Bliss, U. S. A., not long before his death from the yellow fever, sent me the voluminous Transactions of this Society, containing documentary and traditional testimony, with engravings illustrating the history, purpose and appearance of the Old Stone Mill of Newport, which Mr. Touno wished to save from destruction. Mr. Rafn's works, going to establish the ante- Columbian discovery of America by the Scandinavians in the tenth century, and its subsequent colonization, partieuarly in New England, do not derive their validity from this or any other existing monument, but from ancient manuscripts recently discovered, bearing all the internal marks of authenticity as it respects dates, topographical, geographical, nautical, and astronomical descrip-

tion and evidence. Mr. Rafn does not rely on the old Stone Mill's antiquity as in any way essential to his argument, inasmuch as his proots are, independent of this monument, altogether satisfactory. Respecting the Old Structure at Ikrw porl, (the Old Mill), wo refer to an article by Andreas Schmeller, in which he states that he had laid F. Catherwood's drawings of this building before the historical section of the Royal Bavarian Academy of Sciences, which numbers many authorities important on such a question, (Sulpiz Boisseree, Klenze, Thiersch,) who recognized its high ago, and that especially the eminent historians of art, Kai.lenbach, declared it to be in the Roman or ante-Gothic style, and a baptismal chapel belonging to the period of the earlier middle ages. Mr. Rafn and his illustrious coadjutors of the Society will, doubtless, rejoice to dollars Touro's bequest of ten thousand hear of Mr. for the preservation of the Old Mill, as it is called, though, probably, it is an ante-Colnmbian baptismal chapel, corresponding, as it does, with similar structures in the North of Europe, and built by
8 T tho Northmen in what they called Vinland þÿ the Scandinavian name of Massachusetts and Rhode Island more than seven centuries since.

The Law of tho 11th of March 1851 for the Kingdom of Denmark, concerning Transmission by Post of Letters and Packets, is hereby extended to the Danish West India Possessions, in the following manner, and with the modifications contained in this ordinance. ' . The Postage of Letters originating in, and addressed to any place in the Danish West India Islands shall be uniform, without regard to the distanco. Tho present rules for exemptions from paying Postage shall remain unchangod until further. 2. 1 ) The Postage of single Letters shall be 4 Cents, unless Post stamps are affixed to them ; these stamps to bo sold by the Post department, at tho rato of 3 Cents a pieco for a single Letter. Letters weighing one Danish Loth (half an ounoe) or less, shall be considered as single Letters. With rospcct to Letters weighing above one Loth, tho following scale shall be employed, viz : Above 1 but not exceeding 2 Loths : two rates or 2 Post-stamps. Above 2 but not exceeding 3 Loths : three rates or 3 Post-stamps.

Above 3 but not exceeding 4 Loths : four rates or 4 Post-stamps. Above 4 but not exceeding 5 Loths: five rates or 5 Post-stamps. Above 5 but not exceeding 6 Loths: six rates or 6 Post-stamps. Above 6 but not exceceding 7 Loths: seven rates or 7 Post-stamps. Above 7 but not exceeding 8 Loths : eight rates or 8 Post-stamps. And so on, one rate (1 Post-stamp) being added for every Loth up to 32 Loths. 2) For Letters marked Recommended or " "NB" shall be paid, besides the ordinary, an additional Postage of 7 Cents. If, at the request of the sender, the Letter is accompanied by a written acknowledgment of the receipt of the same, to be returned with the signature of the receiver, the sender shall prepay the rate of a single Letter, for the return. 3) Dead Letters, to be returned on demand, and Letters addressed to persons who have changed their residence, shall only be charged with the Postage, that originally should have been paid. 4) Envelops enclosing Letters and other articles sent by the light Mail shall be charged with the same Postage as Letters. 3. For conveyance by the Post of other articles than Letters the following charges shall be paid. A. The light Letter Mail. 1) For Packets in general, not exceeding 32 Loths, shall be charged as for Letters. EVACUATION of LESSER WALLACHIA by hie RUSSIANS. THE SIEGE OF KALAFAT RAISED.

On the 1st April the Russians experienced a considerable check at Czcrrmvoda, and subsequently evacuated Lesser VVallaehia. CzernaVoda is situate between Rassnva and Hirsova, to the west of Kostendjo, in the Dobrudscha. It appears that for the last two months affairs of outposts took place every day, and occasionally sorties of cavalry. The Russians were in the liab't of approaching within reach of cannon shot, showing themselves and parading for a time, firing their carbines, but the moment the fort opened its fire they invariably got very quickly out of þÿharm way. s On the 1st April the Turks made a reconnoissanc# of a more serious kind than usual, to which allusion has been already made. Five squadrons of regular troops and 400 Bashi-Bazouka mounted at two þÿo clock in the morning, and bent their course in the direction of Poiana. The only people they met on the road, which þÿw as cleared by the irregulars, were some Cossack videttes, who galloped at their utmost speed to the camp to give the alarm. The Bashi-Bazouks, who followed hard, arrived at Poiana at the same moment as the Cossacks, leaped the ditch of the camp, and were at four þÿo clock in the town. The regular cavalry, who had increased their speed, arrived in about ten minutes after. The Russians did not by any means expect the attack. They had shown themselves the preceding days, and in considerable force, but were ignorant that the Ottoman general had been aware of the retreat of a part of the force. In fact, there were not at Poiana

more than two regiments of regulars and 400 Cossacks þÿ in all about 1,400 men. The whole of the infantry and artillery, who had been concentrated some short time previous in expectation of an attack, had been withdrawn. The sudden arrival of the Turks threw the small force into disorder and terror. The men rushed in the greatest dismay from the stables, where they found themselves hemmed in by the irregulars. A Russian squadron, which was almost formed, and which was about to issue out for a reeonnoissance, clapped spurs to their horses and fled with the utmost speed. They were charged by the Turks sword in hand, and rout became general. Before they bad time to escape there were about fit) Russians killed and as many wounded, and the Turks returned to Kalafat with a great number of prisoners. Thus the sortie, which was intended only as a reeonnoissance, became changed by circumstances into an attack, and it would have had still greater results if the Turks had had with them a few pieces of artiliery, and above all infantry to enter the houses. The Russians fled, without dia ving bridle, as far as Mugluvit, a small place about t.iree or four miles to the North of Kalafat. On the day but one after the Russians returned in considerable number, not less than lfi,000 men. They were as usual repulsed with cannon. A fusillade of sliai pshooters took place, and lasted five hours, as also several charges of cavalry, but without serious result. For three days after they kept in abuscade with two

field pieces in order to surprise the advanced posts of the Turks. A squadron in patrol service found them out and gave the alarm. Some men of the squadron were killed by cannon shot, but the attack was not followed up Tnese alternations of attack and defence havo not in themselves any great importance, but they covered a progressive movement of the evacuation .by the Russians of Little Wallachia. That is now compete, and the menace i attack on Kalalut is definitively abandoned. MOVEMENTS IN TURKEY. The Himalaya, having 1,850 English soldiers on board, arrived at Constantinople on the 14th, in the midst of the greatest enthusiasm on the part of the population. These are the first European troops who have touched the banks of the Bosphorus since the time of the Crusades. At her departure from Gallipoli, the Himalaya left there French and English forces to the number of nearly 36.000. An Anglo-French division was expected at Adrianople, and 3,000 European soldiers were already established at Bulair, on the road to that ulace, about three leagues distant from Gallipoli. The Ottoman fleet, consisting of eight ships of the line, of which three were Egyptian, and five steam frigates, was w aiting for orders to enter the Black Sea, under Admiral Kaiserli Ahmet þÿl aslia. Mention has been already made of the deputation sent by Schainyl to Constantinople. The object ot the deputation was to obtain arms and ammunition. These have been forwarded to Trebizond, and, in addition, the chiefs of the

army of Asia have received orders to furnish the Circassians with all that they may require. It was Safer Paclia, known for his exploits formerly when chief of the Circassians, who presented this deputation to the Minister of War. Aid was coming in from all sides. Tho son of Abbas Pasha, who is betrothed to one of the daughters of the Sultan, was expected at Constantinople with the princess, his mother. One of the Constantinople letters states that at Bucharest there has þÿ open published an appeal to all the þÿ þÿorthodox populations, from the Emperor of Russia, inviting them to tako up arms against the Anglo-French, who, lie says, are waging war on Russia lor the purpose of destroying the orthodox Church. Another letter says that the capture of a Russian schooner by the Fury was the result of a snare by the Russians, for the purpose of capturing whatever vessel might come near them. When the Fury took possession ot the schooner, a 50-gun frigate, two brigs, and two steamers suddenly issued from Sebastopol, in the liope of capturing the English vessel, but she got clear oft' without damage. The Sidon, Retribution, Firebrand, and Niger steamers, and the French frigate, Magellan, were cruising to intercept five Russian transports, with military tores, from Nicolaview to Sebastopol.

Admiral Napier has formed his fleet into three divisions, but disposed in such a way, and sufficiently near each other, that he can, in case of need, reunite them for battle. The first of these divisions takes up its station near the Gulf of Livonia, and is not far from the ports of Polaudgen, Libau, and Windau ; the second in the same gulf, in sight of the Riga harbour, so that it can prevent all communication by sea ; and the third is placed at the entrance of the Gulf Finland, for the sake of observation, not far from Sveaborg Helsingfors, where the Russian Baltic squadron still keeps close. Two English steamers are cruising pretty near this latter port. The English cruisers have taken several Russian ships, and brought them into Copenhagen þÿ -W .> - Seizure of Two Russian Steamers of War in tee Thames. þÿ Two wooden steam-frigates, nearly completed, in the yard of Mr. Pitcher, at Worthlleet, intended for the Russian government, have been seized by the Customs, m pursuance of an order just issued from her Majesþÿty government. s It appears that, some 12 months since, a contract was entered into between the Russian Consul General and Mr. Pitcher, for the building of two wooden screw-steam-frigates. The work went on, and certain monies were paid on the contract. About two months ago the government communicated with Mr. Pitcher, recommending the discontinuing of the building of the ships. Attempts were then made, as we are informed, to either sell or transfer them

to a neutral power. In the meanwhile the work proceeded ; one ship was so far completed as to lie ready for launching, and the other was in a forward state. The tacts were submitted to the law otlieers of the crown, and after a careful inquiry and consideration of the whole case, the government, on Tuesday, sent down orders tor the sizure of the two ships, and in pursuance of that direction, Mr. Scuulan, of the Customhouse, took possession of the frigates in Nortlifleetyard, and placed oliicers on Board of them, who continue in charge. The machinery for them, of the value of 30,000/, was also seized by the Customs authorities. The vessels are of 1,300 tons, and pierced to carry 28 guns. They are not burned, hut the one ready for launching bears the tigurehead of the Czar. We are assured that the Admiralty did not entertain any negotiation for the purchase ot the steamers.

THE ENGLISH FLEET. The English fleet appeared in the Cattegat on the 14th, arrived in Wmgo Bay on the 17th, and Admiral Napier proceeded thence in the Valorous to Copenhagen, where he landed on the 20th, and there revived despatches at the hands of Mr. Buchanan, which had been waiting for him some days. According to one account Sir Charles proceeded a' once to wait on the Minister of Marine ; another slates that he was about to have an audience of the King. It appears now to be nearly settled that if not the entire English fleet, certainlv the larger vessels, w .11 pass through the Great Be't, and not the Sound, where there is only Irom 21 to 26 feel deptli of water, which is less than the Duke of Wellington, for instance, draws. Not only the Sound, but the whole Baltic up to Stockholm, is free from ice. At Elsinore it is said there is a contract lor the delivery of 50 oxen (carcasses) a-day for the consumption ol the beef-loving British. A number of vessels with coals had also arrived there for the use of the fleet. The Prussian towns on the Baltic are bestirring themselves to avert danger from themselves and tlioir trade. Stralsnnd and Danzig have sent memorials to the King. Several other towns iri Pomerania have joined the Stettin address. The object of all these pet tions is to pray the King to join issue with the Wpstern Powers and not with Russia, for the hostility of the former would be the ruin of Poinerania a. id Ost and West Preussen. The Ice is the Northern Seas þÿ In a letter from

Berlin we have some interesting statements as to the breaking up of the ice on the Vistula, and the probable delay of the thaw in the Gulf of Finland : þÿ It was hoped that the breaking up of the ice upon the Vistula would have taken place without causing damage. This hope has been frustrated. The swollen waters have overflowed their buiks at Schwedt and at Dantzic. At the latter place the dykes have been carried away in some places, and the whole of the meadows called the " Werdes," laid under water. At the former the waters rose from 12 to nearly 19 feet on the night of the 15th, and inundated tlio whole town, doing enormous mischief. The waters have risen 16 inches above the level of the great inundations of 1846, and within four inches of the highest point recorded within the last hundred years. We have had a continuous fall of wet snow difrtng the last 18 hours, and there can be no doubt that, a sort of second winter has set in to the north-east ; so that little chance exists of the upper side of the Gulf ofFinland being free from ice for the next fortnight. This is highly important. It would be a strange coincidence were Providence to ordain that Russia should ere long 6iiffer grievous injury by sea, in part through the ame agency whereby she obtained incalculable advantage by land in 1812. Hamburg letters report the weather in the Gulls as still extremely cold, the thermometer (Reaumur) standing at 10, 12, and 14 degrees of frost. standing at 12 degrees of warmth, a temperature wliicti, if maintained, will soon cause the breaking up of the

FINAL DECLARATION OF PRUSSIA. (BY ELECTRIC TELEGRAPH.) Berlin, March is, 1854. The Minister Presideut, at the sitting of today of the Second Chamber, made the fallowing declaration, viz. : þÿ Prussia adheres to the terms of the Vienna Note, and no measures will be taken without due reference to the interests of the German Confederates. Prussia has already come to an understanding with those States and Austria. The King is strongly impressed with the necessity of endeavouring to preserve Germany from the calamities of war, and to stand by those states whose territories are more exposed to attack than those of Prussia. Prussia will preserve an independent attitude, and will resist every attempt that may be made to influence her conduet, come from what quarter it may. The strength and the sword of Germany will only be employed to defend German interests. The Minister concluded by proposing a loan of thirty million thalers, which is þÿ by an augmentation of taxes. The Monileur publishes the following report to the Emperor from the Minister for Foreign Affairs : " St he : Your Majesty, being desirous of conciliating the interests of commerce with the necessities of war, has decided that, even after the commencement of hostilities, it is advisable to still protect, in as large a degree as possible, the operations which were buiia fide engaged in and in course of execution before the war. It is with that view that I have the honour to submit to your Majesty the draft of a declaration according to Russian vessels a delay of six weeks to take their departure from French ports. This declaration ensures at the same time to these vessels the possibility of their proceeding direct to their port of destination, without being, in the interval, liable to be captured. As to the French subjects who have at present Russian vessels taking in cargoes for their account in Russian ports, I should have desired that the laws of war could permit them to bring these vessels to France. But it would be necessary to accord for their return a protection which would have for consequences to aliow the enemy's flag to navigate without danger during an almost unlimited length of time. Besides, they will not have any other sacrifice to impose on themselves than a reshipment on other vessels not carrying the Russian flag. I am, sire, with the most profound respect, your Majesty's most humble and most obedient servant and faithful subject, " Paris, March 27."

BUILDING DOINGS AND WAGES AT MELBOURNE. The following extract from a letter recently received, aud dated Melbourne, Dec. 1, 1853, gives some account of what they are doing there, " Wages are enormously high still, as emigration þÿD. has fallen off rapidly .Masons, good hands, 42s. per day (not per week) ; and rubble ditto, 35s. ; carpenters, 35s. to 4l's. ; plasterers, 40s. per day. Timber is a little down just now ; bricks ditto, but after Christmas they will be up again. They are at present £14 per thousand ; Countess slates, £50 per thousand They were about six weeks ago down to £35, but are very scarce again. Very large three and four storied stone stores are being erected in all parts of the city and suburbs, and many tine stone mansious. Many a ten-roomed house 1 have seen let at £1,200 per annum ; nothing but a plain hammer-dressed blue stone front þÿ nothing particular about it. Building in stone is frightful, still there is nothing thought of it here : thousands are spent very Ireely. We have a very tine arcade þÿ þÿ cost a little over £30,000 ; and another erect- something like the Lowther ing, which for elegance of design tar outstrips the other. It is estimated to cost £150,000. Tattersal's Grand llorse Bazaar outdoes anything I have yet seen for horses : Tattersal's at home is a mere shed to it. 1 will send you a plate of it when I can send overland. We have also eight churches and chapels erecting at this time of stone and brick, one college, one free church of

Scotland, high school, one opera-house, two bridges, aud two railways making þÿ the posts also being fixed fcr the telegraph to Williamstown, Port Phillip Heads. J. Knight aud Kemp have just got £oU0 for the best desigu for new Government oflices, to cost £150,000, aud expect the contract to carry it out. W e have also a new mansion for the governor, to cost £50,000 ; baths and washhouses, 4.30,000 ; a new custom-house, and many large jobs ; but I have enumerated enough to show you what we are doing, and expect to do, in the building way, in this golden city. II , late of Jay's, lias many things in hand. Amongst others, the railway bridge over the Yarra Yarra He is also building a steamboat for the Gondola Company, which is to run to Cremorne Gardens, very beautifully laid out at Richmond, on the Yarra Yarra. I also expect be will be the contractor for the graud reservoir, to supply this golden city with water; it will be fifteen miles up the Runty River, from .Melbourne, 15,000 acres of land to compose the large and two smaller reservoirs, and will cost over £150,000, and take two years to complete ; so you see we intend improving a little." þÿ Correspondent of the Builder.

Escape of a Snake from a Man's Mouth. þÿ An extraordinary circumstance occurred a few days ago to Jonathan Smith, gunner's mate, who was paid off at Portsmouth, on the 6th May last, front her Majesty's ship Hastings, 72, on her return from the East Indies. He obtained six weeks' leave. On the expiration of that time, after seeing his friends at Chatham, he joined the Excellent, gunnery ship, at Portsmouth. After some time he was taken þÿunwell his illness increased, and he exhibited swelling on his stomach and limbs. þÿ The surgeon considering it arose from dropsy, he was removed to Haslar Hospital, and after much painful suffering, although lie had every attention paid to him by the medical officers of the establishment, he died. Two hours before his death a living snake, nine inches in length, eatne out of his mouth, causing considerable surprise. How the reptile got, into his stomach is a mystery. It is supposed that the deceased must have swallowed the reptile when it was young, drinking water when the Hastings was out in India, as the ship lay for some time at Trimcomalee, and close to a small island, the Snake Island. The crew used very often to find snakes on board. The way tliey used to get into the holes into the forecastle. ship was by the cable, and The through the hawse deceased was 40 years of age. He was intered in Kingstown churchyard. His s remains were followed to the grave by the ship company of the Excellent. þÿ Morning Chronicle.

Fire on board the Steamer "Clyde." (From the Jamaica Morning Journal, April 8.)

We have been favored with the following particulars relative to the recent tire on board the R. M . S. Clyde : þÿ At about 5 o'clock on Sunday afternoon, the Clyde was brought to off Porto Rico, with the view of delivering the mails. The boats with the mail bags had not left above half an hour, before a volume of smoke was seen issuing from the after hold, where the spirits are kept. An alarm of" fire" was immediately raised, when the captain, crew and passengers set to work to bring a sufficient quantity of water to play on the fire, by means of the patent pump; and a constant supply was thus kept up. Finding that the smoke did not abate, orders were given to tear up the flooring of the ladies' cabin. This was done, and an opening made, through which the flames burst to an alarming extent. By this time, Captain Woodward had succeeded in getting near the flames, and by keeping up supply the of water, which was conveyed to the fire by the hose, the efforts that were made to stay the progress of the conflagration were successful, danger was soon over, and by 8 o'clock all fear of the fire being renewed, was stayed. The Clyde then continued on her course. þÿ þÿooo From the New Orleans Picayune.
Message of President PIERCE to the U. S. Congress, relative to the seizure of the Black Warrior.

Washington, March 16, 1854. President Pierce has transmitted the following Message to the House of Representatives in reference to the Black Warrior case : þÿ In compliance with a resolution passed by the House of Representatives, I herewith transmit the report of the Secretary of State containing all the information received by the Department relative to the seizure of the Black Warrior at Havana, on the 28th ult. There have been in the course of a few years past many other instances the commerce, violations of of aggression upon our rights of American authorities of Cuba, and all attempts citizens, and insults to our national flag to by obtain the redress for them have led to protracted and fruitless negociations. The documents in these cases have been voluminous and when they are prepared they will be sent to Congress. Those now transmitted relate exclusively to the seizure of the Black Warrior, and they present so clear a case of wrong that it might reasonably be expected that as full be made for it, as soon this unjustifiable and indemnity should offensive conduct should be made known to Her Catholic Majesty's Government. But similar expectations in other cases have not been realised. The offending party is at our doors, with largo powers for aggression, but none, it is alleged, for reparation. The source for redress is another hemisphere, and the answers made to our first complaints made to the Home Government are but repetitions of the excuses rendered by inferior officials

to their superiors, in reply to representations as to their misconduct. This peculiar situation of parties has undeniably much aggravated the annoyance whioh our oitizens have suffered from the Cuban authorities, and Spain does not appreciate, to the full extent, her responsibility for the conduct of her authorities. In giving very extraordinary powers to them, he owes it to justice and to her friendly relations with this Government to guard with great vigilant against any exorbitant exercise of those

3 © IB D H S£ A7 powers, and in cases of injuries to provide for prompt redress. I have already taken measures to represent to 'the Government of Spain the wanton injury done by the Cuban authorities by the detention and seizure of the Black Warrior, and to demand immediate indemnity for the injuries which have already thereby resulted to our citizens. In view of the position of Cuba, its proximity to our coast, the relations which it must ever bear to our commercial intere-ts, it is vain to expect that a series of unfriendly acts, the infringing of our commercial rights, and and the adop- tion of a policy threatening the honor security of these States, can long consist with peaceful relations. In case the measures I have taken for an amicable adjustment of our difficulties with Spain should unfortunately fail, I shall not hesitate to use the authority and means which Congress may grant to insure the observance of our just rights, or obtain redress for iujuries received, and will vindicate the honour of our flag. In anticipation of that contingency, which I earnestly hope may not arise, I would suggest to Congress the propriety of adopting such provisionary measures as the exigency of the case may seem to demand. Franklin Pierce.

From the Observer, April 2, 1854. THE PASSAGE OF TIIE DANUBE. On the 23d the Russians under Prince Gortschaknff, crossed the Danube from Oltenitza in great force. Whether they attacked the Turks, or the Turks attacked them, does not appear, but a sanguinary battle ensued, in which the Russians were repulsed, with a loss of 3,000. The Turks then retired into their entrenchments; but it is not clear why they retired if they were victorious. It seems certain, howaver, that the Russian force maintained itself in Bulgaria. On the 24th the preparations for the siege of Matschin were begun by the Corps under General Luders, whose force is estimated at 50,000 men.

STATE OF TURKEY. The Retribution found the Sulina mouth of the Danube impassable. The fleet is still at Beieos. The Russian fleet is said to have come out into the Black Sea. The proposal for mixed tribunals excites the discontent of the Mussulmans. The Sampson returned from her cruise, with information that the Russians were abandoning their forts on the east coast of the Black Sea. Souchoum-Kaleh was in flames, and the Circassians were plundering it. The Furious then left to gather further information. The Russ(;in force opposite Rustcbuck is estimated at 70,000 men at least. CONSTANTINOPLE, April 5 There has been a general illumination for five consecutive nights in honour of the late victories over the Russians, after these latter crossed the Danube. A fear was entertained that there would be a rising of the Greeks, and many of them had been ordered away. Tho combined fleets, which left Beikos on the 24th, anchored at Kavarna Bay on tho 26th, a place of excellent shelter against tho prevailing wiiids from E. by S. and S. S. AV. 3 'JT. tempts are being made by the Russians to throw in supplies to their troops now that they have crossed the Danube, and have orders to bring in any Russian vessels they may find so engaged, or within Turkish waters. CIRCASSIA. The English steamer Samson, which had been sounding on the coast of Circassia, returned on the 21st, bringing tidings of a complete victory gained by the Circassians over the Russians. Early in March the Circassians, provided with arms and ammunition, attacked the Russians, and, after a severely contested battle, dro've them into their castles on the coast. These castles were surrounded and repeatedly attacked during four continuous days. Finally, the Russians, fearing to be cut to pieces, blew up their powder magazines, and sought shelter in ships. The captain of the Samson reports that when some Russians had abandoned two block-houses situated on a hill, the Circassians threw themselves on them and cut the whole to pieces. The satire steamer had spoken with a Russian vessel proceeding to Sebastopol, laden with fugitive soldiers. The loss of the Russians had been considerable. The coast of Circassia is at present free from the enemy.

SOMETHING IN THE WIND. The English fleet has, it appears, suddenly left Kjoge Bay, where it had for some time been stationary, and has proceeded in an easterly direction. It would be premature to speculate at this moment on the precise point against which its operations will be directed, but it seems probable that the movement was accelerated by the report said to have been received from the Dauntless, which has been on a cruise in the Gulf of Finland, and which is stated to have observed 18 Russian ships of the line in the harbour of Sweaborg. Rumour adds that a hostile squadron has been seen near the Island of Faroe ; and it may be hoped, therefore, that our sailors will have an opportunity of meeting the enemy under circumstances which will enable our powerful naval force to exert itself to the utmost advantage. It might have been apprehended that Russia would endeavour, as far as possible, to avoid encountering us in the open sea ; but it may, perhaps, have been thought advisable to attack the British fleet before the arrival of the French contingent, which will not bo much longer delayed, and the report to which we refer may not, therefore, he altogether unworthy of credit. A few days will, in all probability, acquaint us with the object and the results of Admiral Napier's movement ; and, in the meantime, we trust to the gallantry of our seamen and the skill of their commander to give a good account of any hostile force which they may encounter.

Various Facts. þÿ Matschin was only captured after a two days' unintermitted bombardment, and its being twice stormed. The garrison, said to be nearly 5,000, were marched under escort into Bessarabia. Amongst them were said to be several. French and English military instructors. It was not a place of any strength, but was well stored iu many ways. Respecting Ilirschova, it seems that the Turkish covering trenches were only taken after a most obstinate defence ; and that Mustapha Pasha, with the covering army, surprised by the Russian passage of the river at Ibrailla, and threatened in flank by the Russian corps just landed from Odessa (where, by the way, were the English and French ships at that time ?) was obliged to abandon Ilirsova to its fate. HOLD ON. The Turks rgjain their strong position at Kalafat, and it is stated that, at the close of last month they successfully assailed and drove back, with 10,000 infantry and 2,000 cavalry, a vastly superior force of the enemy. The central portion of the Danube is not, it would seem, at this moment, the scene of any very active operations, but it is hardly probable that so important a post as Giurgevo has been abandoned by the Russians. With regard to the general prospects of tho campaign, it may be well to remark that a slight acquaintance with the details of former wars will effectually correct any tendency to overrate either successes or reverses on the banks of the river. There is hardly a fortress in its vicinity which was not taken and retaken in the struggles of the last century, without producing any decided effect on the ultimate issue of the contest, or even of the campaign. Kalafat, however, is undoubtedly a position of the highest impot tanec, and we trust that its defenders may verity a saying which the historian of the Ottoman empire attributes to Napoleon : " Let 10,000 Turks be placed within walls, and 100,000 assailants will be needed to drive them out." So long as the western extremity of Omar Pacha's line is free from immediate danger, our chief anxiety will be for the Dobrudscha ; and it is well that assistance is near at hand. General Canrobert, with a portion of the French contingent, arrived at Constantinople ten days ago, and an English vessel, with the 93rd on board, was at

the same time in sight ; and as the allied fleets are in the immediate vicinity of the scene of action, it maybe hoped that the enenty will be kept in check until the arrival of the French and English troops, now rapidly pressing to their destination in the East.

From the Observer' THE SECRET CORRESPONDENCE BETWEEN RUSSIA AND ENGLAND. The Ob- erver presented, exclusively, to the public, the vert important and confidential correspondence and communications that tiave recently taker, place between the Russian Government, the Emperor of Russia in person, and the British Ambassador at St. Petersburg, and the British Cabinet respecting Turkey. We feel ourselves justified, therefore, in again reverting to them for the purpose of placing more clearly before the public and the world the insidious designs of Russia, and the absolute manner in which the stipulations of treaties, and the rights of nations, are set at nought by the Czar, when they stand in the way of his schemes of territorial aggrandisement. It is needless to say that the ambitious designs of Russia are not those of yesterday þÿ that they have been followed up unscrupulously and perseveringly since the days of the Empress Catherine, and that there has been a gradual, but steady process of encroachment upon the Turkish territories, both in Europe and Asia, during more than half a century, with the ultimate object of obtaining possession of Constantinople and the Dardanelles, converting the Mediterranean sea into a Russian lake, and ultimately cutting off the Western Powers, and Great Britain in particular, from all intercourse and commerce with the East. Masked under the flimsy pretext of a friendly visit to this country, the Emperor himself, so tar back as the year 1844, attempted personally to enter into secret

negotiation with the British Government upon the subject of Turkey. The influence and co-operation of the Duke of Wellington was sought for, and representations, couched in the most insidious form, were made to the Government, in order to show that Turkey had been, on all occasions, unfaithful, regardless of treaties and obligations, and that the Porte must not be confirmed in the delusion that it could do so with impunity. It was further argued that the Cabinets of Europe could not see the Christian population of Turkey exposed to flagrant acts of oppression and religious intolerance, without being obliged to interpose on their behalf. Then comes the significant hint that the Turkish empire contains many elements of dissolution within itself, and that it may not be in the power of friendly cabinets to avert its fall. The suggestion is then thrown out, that the danger resulting from this catastrophe will be much diminished if England and Russia came to a previous understanding, as to the eourse to be taken by them, and which will have the full assent of Austria (without asking it), as an entire conformity of principles and action exists between it and Russia. Although the bait was very artfully thrown out, it was distinctly repudiated by England, who unhesitatingly refused to join Russia and Austria in the perpetration of a great political crime, which would form a counterpart to the infamous partition of Poland. England refused to pledge herself to anything beyond communicating to Russia what her intentions

were, in the event of anything unforeseen occurring in Turkey, and this was the sole result of the preliminary negotiations ten years ago, which was embodied in a memorandum presented by Count Nesselrode to the English Cabinet. In the beginning of the year 1853 the subject is again resumed by the Emperor of Russia in person, with our Ambassador at St. Petersburg, Sir Hamilton Seymour. He makes a of previous meeting at the palace the Grand Duchess Helen, arrangement for a and there, in the most gracious manner, addressed the Ambassador, expressing his delight at the formation of the new Ministry, hopes it may long exist, and desires Sir H. Seymour to convey these assurances to the Earl of Aberdeen, with whom lie said he had been acquainted for nearly forty years, and for whom he entertained equal regard and esteem. The ice having of been thus skilfully broken, and the condescension the Czar wound up by shaking hands with the Ambassador, his Majesty was about to withdraw, but Sir Hamilton Seymour, who appears throughout to have acted with the greatest judgment, discretion, and were observed that, as demonstrations straightforwardness, at the time being made towards the south, it would be desiratilo if Ins Majesty would say a few words tending to calm the anxiety with regard to the affairs of Turkey. The Emperor was fairly taken aback ; he stammered and hesitated, but all at once " changed his tone, " and became open and confidential. Stay," said he, we have a sick man upon our hands, a man seriously ill, and it

will, I tell you frankly, be a great misfortune if one of those days lie should slip through our fingers, especially before all the necessary arrangements are made." The inference was obvious, although the Emperor was loo cunning to convict himself further al the moment. It was a covert proposal to arra.ige for the division of the spoil and repartition of tl.e Turkish territories beforehand, but the Ambassador bluntly and honestly repelled it, observing that it was the part of the generous and the strong man to treat with gentleness the sick and feeble man. The Emperor was discomfited, but not displeased. It was his poliey to appear gracious and frank, and the Ambassador records his opinion of the Czar's honesty by stating, at the close of his despatch, that the Emperor's assurances are contradicted by his acts. afterwards Sir Hamilton A few days Seymour was snmmoned to another interview with the Einpcror, and the dying state of the Turkish empire was again re- ferred to. " Close to us," he says, " lies Turkey, and nothing better for onr interests can be desired In her present state of decrepitude she may suddenly die upon our hands ; we cannot resuscitate what is dead, and it is better to arrange beforehand." The Ambassador tory and confidential tone. þÿ still held off, and the Emperor a<rain tried the concilia- " Now, I desire to speak to you as a friend and as a gentleman ; if England and

str m <> a x I arrive at an understanding in this matter, as regards the rest it matters little to me, it is indifferent what others do and think. I tell you plainly, that if England thinks of establishing herself at Constantinople I will not allow it and then he intimates that he himself ma v find it necessary temporarily to occupy Constantinople. There was here a very judicious mixture of threats and flattery, but Sir Hamilton Seymour has penetration enough to see through it, and informs his Government that the subject is one which has occupied the Emperor's thoughts for many years, and to avoid any misunderstanding hereafter lie takes the very necessary precaution of giving Count Nesselrode a correct summary of the conversation. The decision of the British Government upon these propositions, as embodied in the despatch of Lord John Russell, is honest and distinct. He shows evidently and by argument the dishonesty of the Emperor's projects, and shows that the very fact of two of the great powers of Europe arranging beforehand for the partition of Turkey would bring about the very catastrophe which it was apparently intended to avert. The agreement would reach the Sultan's ears, and alarm and " the foresight of the friends of the patient alienate hint, while it stimulated his enemies, adding, would prove the cause of his death." But the Czar is not to be so easily shaken from his resolution, and ill a subsequent interview with the British Ambassador, on the 21st February, he again urges that "the sick man isdying."

Sir Hamilton stoutly denies it, and says countries do not die so easily. Then replies the Einperor, " If your Government has been led to believe that Turkey retains any elements of existence, your Government must have received incorrect information;" headds, that if he could have ten minutes' conversation with Lord Aberdeen, an understanding understanding " between gentlemen" is all that he would be come to. A general would ask. Even at this point of the correspondence Sir H. Seymour is enabled to inform his Government that a scheme for the ultimate partition of Turkey has been arranged between Russia and Austria, to which they invite England to be a party, to the exclusion of France. Throughout he whole of these extraordinary negotiations the Emperor cannot believe that any nation would regret a well organized project for plunder, and, accordingly, he now states plainly to the Ambassador what he expects himself, and what he undertakes England shall have for her share of the spoil if she will join in the nefarious design ? He says he will not tolerate Constantinople being occupied by England, France, or any great power (excepting, of course himself.) But, as Egypt is of importance to England, lie will not object to her taking possession of it, and also of the Island of Caudia. The offer was peremptorily rejected by our Ambassador, who disclaimed on the part of England any ideas upon Egypt, beyond securing a safe and ready communication between British India and the mother country.

Baffled at every turn, a memorandum is then drawn up by the Emperor, in which he labours to show that there were no proposals for a partition, or any binding convention þÿ that it was merely an interchange of opinions. He complains that, while Lord John Russell counsels forbearance towards Turkey, France has been permitted to adopt a different of course, has obtained the admission a ship of war within the and, by menaces, Dardanelles, without any remonstrance on the part of England France being permitted to bully the Porte, he thinks Russia and Austria, are entitled to try the same game, and concludes by expressing his satisfaction that Russia and England are in accord. Sir Hamilton, however, follows up the Emperor through all his windings and trickery, and, in a letter to Count Nesselrnde, points out the errors into which the Emperor has fallen with regard to the policy of England in Turkish affairs. The Earl of Clarendon follows this up by accepting with apparent frankness the last assurances received from the Emperor he repeats that England desires no territorial aggrandisement, and will be i o party to any secret arrangement, and in a subsequent despatch lie suggests the propriety of closing the correspondence. Several subsequent explanations are tendered by the Emperor of his anxiety to preserve the existence of Turkey, and to co-operate with England for that purpose ; but these professions, after the propositions he originally made, will be taken for just what they ate worth. It is evident that no reliance

can be placed upon either his professions or his promises, that he will be ready to take advantage of every opportunity that presents itself sacrifice bounded ambition, at whatever to minister to his un- of honesty and principle, and it is fortunate for the future destinies of Europe that in the war now about to take place thero is such a unanimity of feeling and sentiment on the part of the two great Western Powers, England and France, and such a combination of strength and moderation as, we trust, will enable them to dictate terms to Russia, and enforce their observance.
