THE WAIL General Forey, and the 4th Division of the Army of the East, left Malta, with Ins squadron, on the 22d, in fourteen steamers. and proceeded to the Piraus, with a view of taking possession of that port A body of English Marines, which have been placed under the command of General Fmcy, formed part of the expedition The representatives of France, England. Austria, and Prussia, at Vienna, have signed a new protocol, in order to adapt the Anglo- French Convention and the Austro-Prussian treaty to the engagements entered Into bv the protocol of the 9ih of April. The draught of a note to Russia has been sent by the Con- Icrencc to Berlin for the approval ol the Prussian Government.

On the 25th the Ministers of Austria and Prussia at Frankfort presented to the Diet the joint declaration of Austria and Prussia, announcing the continued cordiality of the four powers, and declaring that the prolongation of the struggle between Russia and Turkey constituted a danger for Germany, and that the integrity of Turkey must be maintained. After this declaration five protocols of the proceedings of the Vienna Conference were laid before the Diet, the fact of the Austro-Prussian Treaty was notified to that assembly, and the other German States were invited to adhere to it. The Russians have been manoeuvring to cut off the communication between Varna and Stlistria To frustrate this design an English division was to embark at Constantinople for Varna, while the Fiench force was to march on the Balkans. The pontoon bridge across the Danube was destroyed by the Turkish artillery on the 18lh The army corps of General Danneberg was thereby prevented from crossing the river. Brisk encounters took place on the 16th at Simnitza, Sistowa, and Rutschuk. at which latter place the Russians made an unsuccessful attempt to cross the river somewhat below Giurgevo Marshal Paskiewitsch, has crossed the Danube, near lvalarasch, and established his head-quarters before Stlistria, which has been closely invested. It is now reported that the Russians, unable, on account of the blockade, to defend the seaboard of Circassia, had evacuated al! their positions from Batoom to Anapa þÿ an

extent of 200 leagues They burned all their own forts and retired to ivutais in the interior The Circassians came down from the mountains, and took possession id all the posts which the Russians had occupied, making prisonets 1,500 men, whom they surprised at Sukkum- Kaleli The Circassians had proclaimed a provisional government, under the presidency of a brother-in-law ol Schamyl. No steamer had arrived at Dantzig from the Baltic Fleet up to Friday, and two weeks' despatches and one mail were waiting there for conveyance. A Greek bishop was arrested in Pestli (Hungary) on the evening of the 18th. as a Russian emissary, and important papers, it is said, were found on his person. The Army of St Outer will he divided into three divisions, and will he extended towards the East. One division will he commanded, as alreadv slated, bv General Baraguav d'Hillers, another by General Pelisser, and the third bv General d'Arbouville. The following is the manner in which the troops that are to be concentrated in the neighbom hood of Marseilles will be distributed. One division will be cantoned at the Pernios, and another in the commune of St. Victoret. between the Pas-des- Lancters and the rnilwnv. These troops will he about 25. 090 in number, it is also in contemplation to quarter a division in Marseilles or the sobuibs, but this has not been definitively decided on. In 1S49, at the tune of the expedition to Rome, one brigade was quartered in the surrounding hamlets, while another was in the town itself. Lastly,
about 15 000 will he encamped at St. Aiaxtm in, this point being convenient lor a sudden embarkation either from Toulon or Marseilles.

Kalafat, May 10. þÿ The day before yesterday six squadrons of Turkish Cossacks and five of Turkish hussars had an engagement with the Russian Cossacks near Radovan. A Yankee Trick. þÿ "One morning, about ten days since, we saw a large vessel some eight or ten miles ahead, which we fully believed to he a Russian man-of-war, as she made all sail to get away, and showed no colours. As we rapidly came up with her, she took in sail, until she was under reefed topsails (fighting trim), so we beat to quarters, and the pipe sounded loudly 'hands bring ship into action.' For about three minutes every thing was hustle, apparently, casting the guns loose, clearing the decks, &c. Five minutes after the pipe every gun was double-shotted and primed, and ihe men standing with the match lines in their hands waiting for the word to fire, and just as we got within good distance the blackguard ran up American colours, and coolly told us he would have hoisted them sooner, but he wanted to see how smart we could clear for action. If our tars did not bless him to the wrong side of Heaven do not believe tne !"

Bains' F.i.ectric Clock. þÿ It was no weight, no spring, no escapement, no winding up, no agency in itself for putting or keeping the hands in motion. In a garden is dug a hole four feet deep, into which is thrown a layer of coke then a layer of earth, and then a few zinc plates. A feeble but constant current is generated hv the contact of the earth with the coke below it and the juice above it, without the aid of any other battery : and this current is conveyed in doors by copper wires from a coil round a magnet ; ami the electro magnet thus formed is made to constitute the boh of tbe pendulum of the clock. Delicate and beautiful mechanism enables the electric apparatus to give a vibratory motion to the pendulum, and the pendulum in its turn to give motion to the two hands of the clock. By an occasional feed of zinc to the earth's battery, opcc in three or four years, is all that is access tv to give to this Clock a sort of Perpetual Motion.

From the Observer , May 2lsL THE BALTIC. Ail was well with the Amphion steam frigate, 34, Captain Key, up to the 12th instant. On that day the Amphion anchored off Memel, sainted the Prussian flag with 21 guns, and seemed for the moment o have nothing so much at heart as the procuring of water and provisions. The fleet was seen on the 7th, south of Gottska Sandoe, steering south-eastwards, as was supposed for the purpose of falling in with the French fleet; the latter left Hirtsholm on the 11th, sailing southwards. On the 7th, in the afternoon, an English ship of the line was towed out from Landsort by a steam corvette, and shortly afterwards a steam corvette ran in. On the following day the liner and the corvette that had remained behind at Elfsnabben put out to sea. Advices from Copenhagen of the 1 3th state that intelligence had reached there from Gothenburg of an English steam-sloop, of 3 guns, name not mentioned, having brought in two Finland brigs, laden with salt. These two prizes had been taken by the Bulldog, and passed over to the Alban, whose more special task it is just now to lay down buoys and other sea marks where they have been removed. On the 9th, late in tbe evening, the Holyrood, Captain Lovett, arrived at Elsinore, trom Sheerness, with provisions for the English fleets The Tartar (or Tartarus) four guns, Lieutenant Risk, is reported as between Heligoland and NVanger Oog, off the mouths of the Elbe and Wezer, so as to leave little chance for any Russian property to run out with impunity. On the 9th inst. the steain-

corvette Cruizer left Memel. Travellers coming direct from Riga state that great exertions are being made to strengthen the old batteries, and to erect and arm their works at the entrance of the river, and that vessels laden with sand have been sunk in the channel, and numerous other precautions taken, to prevent war vessels gaining access to the town. On the 2nd, the Catharina Charlotte was despatched under the guidance of Captain Wright to Hull. On the 7th the Prussian frigate Gefion, 48, Commander Schroeder, anchored in the roads of Dantzig, the harbour not admitting of a vessel of 18 feet draught of water entering ; and on tho following day the Mercur joined her. The following are extracts from a letter received at Devonport from an officer on board her Majesty's ship, in the Baltic, dated 1st of May : þÿ " I do not know when there will be another chance of sending a letter, as there is no knowing what our movements will be. All I can say is, that at present we are waiting for the ice to break up in the Gulf of Finland, when we shall commence operations in a true English style, and no flies. We have succeeded in capturing a few prizes, in all about twenty-five ; but 1 am afraid we (the ) will only share in two, not being present in this capture of more, so that our share of prize money will not be much. But still every little is a help; andast.be war is not yet over by a long way, there is no knowing what may turn up for tho old bird of prey. I am very well, but the cold is awful.

The sun is warm, but it is tbe wind that one feels so much ; but one can't grumble, for we have had some beautiful weather, and on the whole have been very comfortable and happy. The fleet are longi ng to have a crack at something, and are in the highest spirits about it, but the Russians are such cowards that we are peilectly unable to get at them, unless we go right in tho lion's mouth, by passing some awful strong forts. But old Charley intends doing something in that way, and is only waiting for a chance, when 1 iiope the English fleet will give them something that they won't forget in a hurry. On the 28th we were cruising off the Island of Gottska sands, just opposite the Gulf of Finland, waiting for tho fleet to join tis, as we have been sent away on a cruise since the 21st nit. The admiral, Sir Charles, did a very shabby thing the other day. VVe were cruising, the whole lot of us together, when he divided us into three divisions, and sent us away to cruise. When we were all out of his sight he set sail with his own squadron of the fleet, and tried to go and capture a fort in the Gulf of Finland. To our great delight he had to return, not being able to get in on account of the ice ; so he whs rather sold, after all the precautions he took of sending the other admirals awav . In the Gulf of Finland we picked up the French ship which has been knocking about up here trying to p '< up the fleet. She is like ourselves, waiting the arrival of the commander-in-chief. She is a beautiful ship,

but I'd back our 90's against her. We muster strong up here þÿnow about 35 to 40, and expect more to join us every day. We expect ten more French to join us, besides several more of our own. It will be a grand sight when we all muster together Only just wait until our return to England, with each of us having some unfortunate vessel in tow There's a good time coming yet. April 30, at anchor, Stockholm, Sunday. þÿ We have just arrived here after knocking about ever since in some of tho most beastly weather one would wish, nothing but a thick heavy fog, and rain, and a wet jacket to boot. I am not at all sorry I am in port again, for I am almost worn off my legs. I have not had a line yet from England, but I am jolly well sure it is not any fault at home. Tho whole fleet are in a similar position Our letters must be knocking about somewhere, and a jolly batch there must be somewhero for us. May 1 þÿ The bag closes this forenoon, sol must conclude. The Conflict has not yet arrived. The Odin steam-frigate took a prize yesterday, with £8,000 on board. We are rather annoyed about it, as we must have passed her." A private letter trom an English gentleman now cruising " The in fleet in the Baltic now 13 45 sail, 2,250 guns, his yacht in the Baltic says : and about 23,400 men ; this is inclusive of the French fleet of five ships of the line, foil' frigates, and four steamers. I don't think Cronetitft or weahorg will

8 !fc <0 at JE A'TJS. bo bombarded; they are in such difficult channels that, without tho steam power, it would be quite impossible to get into position to attack, as stone walls and casemated batteries must be fired at from not more than 200 yards distance. No doubt an attack on Sveaborg might and would be entirely successful, but of course not without severe loss and much damage to our ships; immediately after which, out would come the untouched Russian fleet, of 27 sail of the line and 38 large frigates, from Cronstadt, and fall on our disabled fleet. Napier is bold enough, but if the Russians expect him to commit some rash folly through love of fighting they are much mistaken. The St. Jean d'Acrc, Capt. Keppel, 'tis unquestionably the finest and most efficient ship here þÿ 91 heavy guns, on two clear fighting decks. The Austerlitz, the only Frenchman in this quarter yet, is a very fine ship, the men very clean and smart aloft. We have not seen their target practice. Their great gun exercise is not so quick as ours, the command being ' un, deux, tkoix,' instead of 'one, two.' I don't expect to go home before next month, but hope to see something worth seeing before I leave."

From the St. Thomas Times, June 17 th- COMMUNICATED. Under slavery the system for governing these Colonies and preserving order was necessarily one of force, and in some measure of arbitrary force. The abolition of slavery carried with it as an immediate consequence the termination of that system and the predominance of law. An absolute condition for a peaceable dominion of the law is a general acknowand in the present instance (although in itself still ledgment of the natural equity of the existing of laws, greater consequence) the public confidence in the abilities and good will of those to whom the application of the laws is intrusted. It is on the second subject that we wish to offer a few remarks. To qualify a person to fill a judicial situation, two things are preeminently required, þÿviz a full knowledge of the law, and a sufficient acquaintance with the language, manners and general character of the inhabitants of the country, in which he is to exercise his functions, the practical state of agriculture, trade, &c. Applying these propositions to our own case, we observe, that the acquirement of the knowledge of law demands an education during many years in the Mother-country, while the second requisite named pre-supposes not merely a sojourn of a certain duration in the Colonies, but also during this period an intercourse with the inhabitants in the practical affairs of daily life and business. In other words the individual is to be first educated in Denmark, and then to spend a certain period of activity in the Colonies, before he can be fit to per-

form the duties we now speak of. Now it is evident to every body acquainted with these Colonies, that it is a thing hardly to be thought of, that any resident here would send a child of his to Denmark for a time of ten to fifteen years, to 6tudy the law with a view of spending his life here until he can be appointed to one of the judicial situations that may happen to become vacant hereafter. At the present moment we think we may venture to say, that not one child or youth born in these islands is residing in Denmark for such a purpose, and from an earlier period, there is but one among the gentlemen holding or aspiring to legal appointments here, who ib a native, the only other individual of this description having lately resigned his temporary appointment and removed himself and family to the Mothercountry, preferring the chances of promotion there to that w# must look exclusively to natives of the Mother- i and not getting a sale when fresh, they were those opening themselves here. It is therefore evident country 10 fill the situations of judges, lawyers, &c. It is furthermore a fact, that of late a complete change has taken place, with regard to the settlement of such gone through the course of their studies and examina- tively considerable number of young men, who had I the Opinions persons in the Colonies. In former times a comparations came out here, beginning their career either as practitioners or þÿKing s clerks, and by gradually acquiring an intimate acquaintance with the language

and the state of the Colonies, took their chances of being promoted into vacant offices. Whatever causes may have operated the change, certain it is, that for a considerable time no such arrivals Imve taken place, and there is no gentleman of the profession residing in the Colonies, who has coine among us later than ten years ago, neither is it at all probable that this state of things is merely accidental and transcient. It becomes thus a question of more or less importance to every individual residing in the Colonics, and according to the extent of his interest, but most particularly to those permanently bound to the country by the possession of immoveable property, what the prospects are of the Colonies being in future provided with legal functionaries properly qualified for their trusts. We þÿ beg in þÿfuture and þÿ to lay due stress on the two adjectives employed properly þÿqualified. There exists at present a limited number of gentlemen here with the proper qualifications, but it is only the other day that we have seen, how ready they are to quit whenever circumstances give them an opportunity of doing so. With regard to toe future we have no doubt, that there will not be wanting those, who having absolved their studies and examination will be willing enough to go over the seas, to' get living ; but a will they be of a kind to prove a benefit to those they go to ? In looking to the probabilities of procuring individuals who are to come here, not to acquire experience but already provided with that experience j cal men to keep it in check. which is an indispensable condition for tho adequate performance of their duty, our expectations are any thing but sanguine. For the information of our readers in England and in the neighbouring Colonies, we give an account of the spread of the Cholera, and of the steps taken to relieve the sufferings of the poor, and to check its total effects. It first appeared, on the 14th of last month in a wooden hovel in a street running into Baystreet, not far from the hospital. A black woman died there from it after a few hours illness, and two other deaths within three days. In the next house but one another person was seized soon alter with the same symptoms. And then a white young woman, Alias Newsam, and afterwards her sister, fell victims. It has been said that it was brought to Barbados from Jamaica, where it is prevailing in the Derwent; that some seamen on board of her died of it on the passage, and the clothes of two of them belonging to this place were brought here and given to the person to be washed, in whose house it first broke out. But the truth of the statement has not been ascertained. On the occurrence of the first cases, the symptoms were not considered by the Medical men to be those of Asiatic Cholera. It was thought to be only an aggravated form of common diar- I rl)a»u, the Health Commissioners lost no tune in cautioning the inhabitants against anything likely to bring on complaints of the bowels, and recommended the adoption of means for the prevention of the spread of the disease. Just before the alarm was given by the sudden deaths of these people in this part of the
City, we may observe, large quantities of flying fish were commonly sold, in a half-putrid state, in the mornings, which were caught into the Careenage by the boats the evening before,

got rid of 10 or 12 for a penny in the morning. So that the caution against the use of any uu wholesome diet was much required. differed about the character of disease, which soon however showed that it was epidemic, in the first week. The number of cases and deaths incieased ; and they were mostly found among the black people, and in the filthiest and closest parts of the Town. From the Bay the disease spread into the close lanes in White Bark arid about St Mary's. A meeting of the Board of Health was again held, and the j fearful truth could no longer be disguised or denied, that Asiatic, or at any rate a most fatal type of Cholera, prevailed in Bridgetown Persons were seized suddenly in the streets and at their business, and after a few hours stupor, attended with cramps in the arms and legs, sometimes with vertigo, died, often without any signs of pain The remedy found most efficacious was Camphor, which administered to a person when first seized, I 2 drops on a bit of sugar in a leiispoonful of water, as recommended by the Homcepnihs, very often was sufficient to arrest the disease. At a later stage it was more obstinate ; and other remedies were resorted to. but by no means with the same success. We seem ns ignorant indeed ol the treatment ol the disease, in its lull development, as of its origin and nature At the end of the second week it was manifested from the increasing number of deaths, that the Epidemic was fast spreading, and becoming, like a conflagration in a City,

too extended for the limited number of medi- 1 he eyes of the public were at length opened to the reality nr.d extent of the danger, when they saw the numerous corpses carried through the streets, Minister of Finance, that he had considered himself 1 five and six, in the same hearse, with no funeral procession, like so much merchandize, j under the care of the Undertaker alone consigned to the grave. The burials were too numerous to be admitted into the Church and to have the funeral services performed over them. Their interment was left to be provided for by the Sexton, the Undertaker, and the Grave Jiggers. The Clergymen turned their attention from the dead to the living. Thev went about visiting the sick, with restoratives in their pockets, and relieving the destitute. The interments were made in the ground of St. Leonard's, a recently erected

corpses Chapel, in the Westbury Hoad. a few were buried there in Over 400 days. The soil being of marl the graves could not without great labor be carried to a depth of six feet ; and sometimes two coffins were put into the same grave The smell arising from the ground became so offensive, that the Grave Diggers could no longer stand it. All the houses in the immediate neighbourhood were deserted. St. þÿLeonard was s becoming a seat of pestilence, and it was found necessary to provide another burial place. On the same road, near the beach, between Brandon's bathing house and Fontabelle, four acres of land was procured, and the interments were removed there from St Leonard s They had now reached the frightful number of 200 in one day. INDIAN RtVRR June 6th 133 7lh 19» 8lh 132 9th (8 þÿo clock p m. 200 In the mean time the authorities have used every exertion to provide against the effects of this dreadful calamity. The Governor has not spared himself neither has any officer even in the humblest grade. The Members of the Board of Health, the Health Commissioners. the Cletgy of the þÿ1 own, und various individuals have devoted themselves with the most admirable courage to relieve the sufferings of those attacked with the disease, and to remove the panic which seizes upon others ; for many have all the symptoms merely from excess of fright, and depression of spirits; and many desert their neighbors and even their relatives, when attacked, and leave them to their late, or to the benevolent attention of strangers, through fear of themselves falling victims to it. Upon the Health Com- of missioners has devolved the chief duty providing for the safely of the it town, with whatever success hitherto, cannot be and denied that they have spared no exertion. Indeed they appear to have taken too much on their shoulders, by offering themselves to become house to house visitants, and to administer medicine to the sick. Through their over exertions several ol them have actually exposed themselves to attacks ol the disease. This is a subordinate duty, requiring strong nerves and robust health ns well as experience, and should be lelt to be performed by those who are not burthened with other duties of a not less important description. I he

Boaid corisisis of nine members; the four Representatives of the City, and of the Rural part ol the Parish; the Rector, the Churchwarden, and three members of the Vestry. The City has been divided into four districts, which are assigned each to two Commissioners ; and the Rural part of the Parish forms another, which is given to two Commissioners also, with the aid of two other gentlemen. In each district theie is a depot for the distribution of medicines and food, the latter given, either cooked or in a raw slate, as required by parties applying. other The ol applicants are authorized by one or the Commissioners. who also give orders for Coffins and Hearses. They employ persons to visit the sick from house to house, administering the medicines directed by the Medical Men, of whom there are two also appointed to each district. The poorer classes are those amonst which the disease prevails most ; and the sick require to be provided with food, as well as medicine. It has also been thought necessary to make arrangements for thinning

the occupants of houses, in which it appears by pitching tents for them, and procuring accommodation otherwise. All this has to be done at the public, expense, and to be provided for by the Health Commissioners. There is no calculating the cost at the present moment, but it cannot fail to be very great. The new Burial Ground alone cost $2,400, and a like sum we may put down for the cost of the Coffins, the conveyance, and the interment of those who have been already buried. But this is not the time to count the cost ; let us be thankful that the Island Treasury is able to meet it ; and let us trust it will serve for the protection of the lives of the inhabitants, from a dreadful calamity which it is beyond the power of man to avert or resist, The benevolence of individuals lias come in aid of the demands of the public funds for the relief of the sufferer!) A very handsome subscription of nearly 1000 dollars lias been raised bv private contributions at the suggestion of the Officers of H. M. Troops at St. þÿAnns i , n which the gentlemen of the Colonial Bank, and the Merchants of the City very liberally assisted. This money it was thought fit to set apart to remunerate the exertions of persons who were employed to go about distributing the homeeopathic remedies, which are generally esteemed the most efficacious, and to supply food and medicine to those in want of them. We may observe however, that the use of camphor, which is the chief restorative, is not confined tollomoio

pathists ; neither is the discovery of its value in Cholera due to the new system ; for it is equally used and has always been employed as a powerful restorative, long before the practice of Homoeopathy came into vogue. The deaths in comparison to the number of cases reported by the Police has not exceeded 50 per cent ; up to yesterday morning 1470 cases were reported, and 745 deaths. The mortality amongst the prisoners in the Gaol in Bridgetown has been most frightful. þÿ The Cholera has proved a General Gaol delivery. There were 156 prisoners of all descriptions confined there. As soon as the epidemic appeared amongst them, the Governor ordered all those confined for debt, to be released, those confined for want of sureties, and for breaches of the peace ; keeping only such as had been convicted of grave offences. The number of these was reduced by sending some of them away to the otiier places of confinement in the rural districts. Some 64, remained behind; of these 49 are already dead and the remaining 15 are all on the sick list. Of those who were sent away 5 died at Moncrief (District C.) and one at (District A.) At the Lunatic Asylum, which adjoins the District A Station House there have been 4 deaths. The Police have also been attacked, but have not suffered so severely. At the Garrison 3 men of the 1st W. I. Regiment have died, and 3 women, and 15 military laborers, the latter Orderlies, waiting upon the Staff Officers, and living mostly at their quarters in the suburbs of the

Town. These men are all Africans, and as soon as they are seized, they obstinately refuse to take any medicine, being quite content to die, and to return as they say to their own country. Amongst the white troops we have heard of only one death, a private in the Artillery. In the out parishes the disease has not been attended with equally fatal effects. It has appeared in most of them, if not all ; but with few deaths. The Vestries have appointed Committees to visit in the several districts of each parish, established depots for the supply of food and medicine, and enlisted house-to-house visitants to report cases as they occur. This has been done in St. Philip where only one case at Congo Road is reporled, and that was promptly and successfully treated by Dr. Gittens. In St. þÿJoseph i s n the vicinity of Bathsheba, considered one of the healthiest parts of the Island þÿ strange to say, the disease has been more prevalent and more fatal than elsewhere in the country, 50 cases and 31 deaths have occurred there, reported fn us by Mr. Kerr the manager of Joes River who is i the visitor of that district. Fortunately they have the 1 services of Dr. Walcott at hand who is at present residing at Bathsheba ; and the attention of the Rector has been also unremitting. Of these cases a large number has been amongst the class of poor whites. Mr. Kerr says the disease was brought from town ; and we fear that has been the case generally in the country districts. Among the deaths, in St. Joseph, is that of Mr. B.

Mayers, proprietor þÿofDACREs estate, at the very advanced age of 86. Another aged victim is we regret to Bay, Mr. Clinckett, the Kditor and Proprietor of the Barbadian newspaper. He was taken on Tuesday evening and died the following day, having been seen in his usual health and spirits at the Commercial Ilali, the same day he was taken, and stopping in his Chair, for the old man was loo infirm to walk, at friend þÿ þÿBowen s to chat with his clerical and Broadstreet acquaintance. The old gentleman and ourselves were frequently at variance in opinion concerning the events of the day ; hut having had the pleasure of a personal acquaintance with him and the several members of his family for many years, we willingly pay a tribute of respect to his memory, as the consistent advocate ol religion and morality, and of the interests of the Church, by whose Ministers and those who sympathised with these principles, his paper was supported. He too was an octogenarian, and has left a widow and four children; one son the Rev. George Clinckett, whom Sir Charles Grey appointed to a curacy in Jamaica some few years ago, and 3 daughters ; two here unmarried, and one in St. Kitts, the wife of Hr Major a Clerk in ihe Colonial Bank

From the Observer. THE SOVEREIGNS OF RUSSIA. The Empress Catherine. þÿ Peter the Third was married Catherine, daughter of to the Prince of Anhall-zerbst, who had then scarcely completed her sixteenth year. They goon began to hale one another with mortal antipathy, for she possessed a bold, undaunted spirit and a masculine understanding, while he was coarse, grovelling, and mean, with no spark of royalty in his composition. He gave himself up to low society and the most scandalous excesses, while she, stung by her husþÿband s brutality, became still more openly indecorous in her conduct. Peter indulged his habitual drunkenness and debauchery to such an extent that he must have been deranged ; he at length became so infatuated with his disgust for Catherine and his passion for one of his mistresses, the Countess WoronzofT, that he determined to divorce and imprison the former, and raise the latter lawfully to his bed and throne. Informed of his designs, Catherine promptly took the initiative, and carried a grand coup d'etat. She caused her husband to be seized and sent as a prisoner to a small palace about 20 miles from St. Petersburg, where he was speedily despatched with the connivance, if not at the positive command of the Empress. This occurred in July. 1762, a little more than a year after they had ascended the throne, and in the coui se of next month Catherine was solemnly proclaimed and crowned Empress of all the Russias. Loud Hozannas pealed the heaven from the mouths of millions, and ambassadors from every potentate in Europe knelt at the

fool ot a ihrone polluted by lust, intemperance amt murder. Yet she ruled well and wisely, following in the footsteps of Peler the Great, with measureless schemes of ambition on the one hand, and of endless projects of improvement and of colonization on the other- She patronized learning, encouraged education, affected philosophy, ordered a te Deum, when SuvarotT butchered 30,000 Turks at Ismail, ami converted each of her palaces into a monster seraglio. Immersed in pleasure, she never neglected business, and died with perfect composure and a tranquil conscience, surrounded by the great officers of state, the members of the Church, and the familiar associates of her domestic orgies. Such was Catherine, the grandmother of the present autocrat Nicholas. She reigned 34 years, and died at the ripe age of 67. The list of Iter pesonal favourites is innumerable, but of those Prince Potemkin exercised (he largest sway, and was the most remarkable as enjoying the greatest power and influence. He was the richest subject in Europe, and died (bv accident) in a ditch. The Partition or þÿPoland. During the reign of Cmherine the Second wee conceived,

digested, and perpetrated, the most atrocious political enormity which sullies the pages of European history. As Talleyrand said afterwards. on another lamentable occasion, the mistake was, if possible, greater than the crime. France and England could have prevented this foul act; but blind to the rights of humanity and their own transparent interests, these two great nations closed their eyes in fatal supineness, while an ancient, independent nation was swept from the map of Europe, without an assigned cause or even a plausible pretext. The idea was first suggested by the Machiavelian brain of Frederick the Great. The tigress of the north responded to it with a convulsive spring, and the gentle Maria Theresa, after a little hesitation, consented to share in the anticipated plunder. Austria and Prussia had long been deadly enemies, and both hated Russia even beyond the detestation they cherished for each other. Yet they made common cause, conspired against a country they were each pledged to protect, and with a shameless profligacy became leagued in a scheme of robbery on a scale of unprecedented grandeur, consummated by the sacrifice of half a million of lives. The Emperor Paul þÿ Paul succeeded to the throne of Russia on the death of Catherine the Second. At that tjme the empiie had increased to 18,000,000 of square miles, comprising 33,000,000 of inhabitants. > The latter had more than doubled since tha accession of Peter the Great, during ihe lapse of a century. Paul was born on tbe 1st of

October, 1754, and, consequently, was 42 at his accession. His parents had but one other child, a daughter, named Anne, who died in early infancy. He was twice married By his first wife, Nathalie, Princess of Hesse- Darmstadt (who died in 1776) he had no family. By his second. Maria, Princess of VVortemburg (who died id 1828) he had len children, four sous and six daughters, smong whom were Alexander, late Emperor, born 1777, died 1825; and Nicholas, the present Emperor, born in 1796. Paul was eager for war. The doctrines of the French Revolution disgusted him; as a genuine autocrat, he held democratic principles in abhorrence, and had no sympathy for freedom of thought or action in any but himself. When Jtbe Emperor Francis appealed to his assistance, he very willingly despatched Suvaroff with 25,000 men to sweep like a simoom across the north of Italy, while, at the same time, he sent 18,000 more to co-operate with the English in their projected expedition to Holland in 1799 He held the soldiers of western Europe in little estimation, and thought, with Caesar, that his Russians had only to come, see, and þÿconquer. Suvaroff was nearly ns mad as his Imperial master; but he possessed a military genius peculiar to himself nione, and quite beyond the reach of ordinary criticism. Wc should think more highly of Suvaroft as a military chieftain, if we could expunge from his history the sanguinary leaf which records the butcheries of Ismai! and Warsaw, on each of which occasions thirty thousand help-

jess beings were slaughtered in cold blood when all resistance had ceased. His despatch, announcing the taking of Ismail, is the shortest on record, and was couched in a couplet, for he was a poet as well as a conqueror. The literal translation runs thus : þÿ þÿ Glory to God and the Empress! Ismail s

ours" þÿ a volume of blasphemy and carnage compressed into nine short words. þÿ The Campaign in Holland. The illdigested campaign of Holland, in 1799, beheld English and Russian troops, for the first time, acting in concert. The fraternisation mixed up badly, and both parties soon entertained mutual dislike, mistrust, and contempt. The Russians were clumsily commanded, and went on headlong like blind buildings without plan, concert, or support, until beaten back again, when they plundered and burnt all that fell in their way, people, animals, and habitations, on the right and left, in the front and rear. They resembled the Free Companies of the middle ages, in courage, license, and ferocity. It was difficult to form any opinion of their generals, who appeared to concentrate all their notions of strategy in a rush and a þÿHoorah! Hermann was taken prisoner in the first engagement, and Essen, his successor, said little, and did less T he combined force was under the nominal control of the Duke of York ; but, by the sapient ordination of the Ministry, and as if to show that they had no confidence in their own selection, he wus forbidden to venture on any movement of importance without the previous sanction of a council of war ; the most improved method of reducing a commander-inchief to a cypher, and of augmenting the probabilities of failure. To the British Cabinet, therelore, and their council of war, must be attributed the ill-lortune which attended all the operations after the successful landing at

the Helder, and the capture of the Dutch fleets in the Texel. Eccentricities or Fall. þÿ His wild eccentricities would hqve been sometimes amu sing, but that they were never divested of cruelty or mischief. Coming down the street railed the Perspective, he perceived a nobleman, who was taking his walk, and had slopped to look at some workmen who were planting trees by the þÿmonarch s order. " What are you doing," said the Emperor, Merely seeing the men work replied the þÿ nobleman, þÿ Oh, is that your employment? Take otF his pelisse, and give him a spade ! There, now work yourself!" The present Emperor Nicholas, some lime since, driving along in his droshky, observed an English gentleman move down another street, apparently, ns he thought, to avoid him. He sent an officer to ask him why he had done so, when the Emperor was coming ? The answer was, þÿ That he did not see hi imperial Majesty " þÿ Then desire him to wear spectacles in þÿfuture, was the immediate command, with which the delinquent was forced to comply during the remainder of his residence at St- Petersburg, much to his own annoyance and the amusement ol his friends, for he was a remarkable well-looking man, and piqued himself on his clear sight. I he present Emperor has always been accounted the finest looking man in Europe, and Alex ander excited much admiration from his prepossessing exterior when he visited England in 1814. Their sister also, the Duchess of Oldenburgh, was approved of even by the fastidious taste of George the Fourth. The

Caimucks are a hideous race, but the physiognomy of Paul far exceeded ordinary Catmuck ferocity and brutish expression. When enraged, he lost all command of himself, which occasionally gave rise to ludicrous scenes. The courtiers knew very well when

atis, the storm was gathering, by a trick the Emperor had in those moments of blowing from his under lip against the end of his short nose. In the rare intervals of better temper, his good humour was betrayed by about in way of swinging his legs and feet an uncouth walking. Upon these occasions his conver. sation was silly, and too grossly indecent to be listened to by ears polite. If women were present his language became more offensive than ever. The dress of Englishmen, in particular, was regulated by the police. I hey were ordeied to wear a three-cornered hat, or. ns a substitute, a round hat pinned up with thice corners, a long queue, measured to the eighth of an inch, with a curl at the end ; » single-breasted coat and waistcoat ; buckles at the knees, and in the shoes, instead of strings. Orders were given to arrest any person who should be found wearing pantaloons. An English servant was dragged from behind a sledge and caned in the streets, lor having loo thick a neckcloth, and if it had been too thin, that pretext would have been useu lor a similar punishment. Alter every precaution, the dress, when put on, never satisfied the police or the Emperor þÿ either the hat was not straight, or the hair was too short, or the coat was not cut square enough. A lady, at courti wore her hair rather lower on the neck than was consistent with the ukase, whereupon she was ordered into clo«e confinement, and to be fed on bread and water. A gentleman » hair fell a little over his fotehead while dan-

cing at a ball, upon which a policeman, wiih loud abuse, told him that il he did not instantly cut his hair, he would find a soldier who should shave his head. When the ukase first appeared concerning the form of the hat, the son of an English merchant, with a view to baffle the police, appeared in the streets of St. Petersburg at having on his head an English hunting cap, sight of which the authorities weie puzzled. ? What could this mysterious integument he It was not a cocked hat," they said ; þÿ neither was it a round þÿhat. In their embarrassment, they reported the allair to the Emperor, who was as much conlouuded us his officials. A new ukase became indispensable. Accordingly, a fresh ordinance wus promul gated, and levelled at the hunting cap ; hut not knowing how to describe the anomaly, the decree announced that no person, on pain of death, should appear in public with the thing on his head worn by the merchant's son. An order against wearing hoots with coloured tops was most rigorously enforced The police officers stopped a foreigner driving through the streets in a pair ol English top boots. This gentleman expostulated with them, saying that he had no others, and certainly would not cut off the tops of Ins hoots. as he sat in bis droshky, Upon which the officers, each woi seizing fell to k and a leg, drew off his boots, leaving him to go burelooted home. All letters were opened, and il they contained any unintelligible or difficult passage, it was immediately construed into direct
treason, and the writer hurried to Siberia without examination. It was impossible that this state of affairs could last long.

'Phis system of extorting from 100 to þÿ. tOOper cent from the public, for lottery tickets, has now become quite a trade to many persons, who devote the greater or entire part ot their time to this business. 'Phis money flows into and benefits foreign countries ; while but a few þÿ persons here are now and then gainers, which circumstance only serves to increase the speculative mania in others. The only effectual means to put a stop

to this, would be to establish our own lottery, which would prevent speculation in tickets, as people could then purchase them without agents. The accounts received from the abovenamed place, by post, are sad, indeed, as to the fatal rapidity with which Cholera is destroying the inhabitants. A correspondent writes us, under date of the 29th May : þÿ þÿ You ask me to write you about the ' Cholera; my report is a sad one; the disease continues to mow down the people, and God knows how þÿ left to record its ravages up to yester many will be day (the 28th May), out of our small population, seventy have been called to their final account, and there are many lingering between life and death. The disease is more rapid in its effects Ibis visitation, than it was in 1850, four or five hours seem to lie the time that the patient lasts. I cannot help, expressing my sense of the attention which our medical man, (the only one in a circuit of 13 miles), Dr. Bayley, is devoting to the | people þÿ up at all hours and at every call. If medical skill and unremitting kindness could check the progress of the scourge, I should have to give a different and more pleasant account. is that suggestby the Central Board of Health þÿ it has a good effect in several cases where it has been administered with promptitude and fare, unfortunately, the people neglect the preventive means, and

when the disease pets into the system, it leads rapidly to dissolution. As you may suppose, our little village is enveloped in gloom, and each man is waiting for the þÿend. Our readers, no doubt, remember the tearful havoc that was committed in 1850, not only at 8t. þÿAnn liny, s but at a small village called the Prio'ry, about two miles from the former place; we sincerely hope that the disease may be stayed in its fearful progress, and that our next accounts may not prove as distressing as that which appears to have existed when our correspondent wrote as above. ST THOMAS IN THE VALE. We regret to state, that Cholera has extended its ravages to þÿ ount þÿDiablo i district, that is, from the settlements at the foot of the Hill, up to the line of the parish of St. þÿAnn s, near the summit. Never, since the death of Dr. A. I,. Palmer, has the inhabitants felt so much sorrow, as at present, for a medical gentleman who was as kind, charitable, and attentive, as Dr. Palmer, has just been laid beneath the earth. At five þÿo clock, on Saturday last, Dr. Brooks paid his last visit to a person dying of Cholera. At that time, the premonitory ( symptoms that were on him during the early part of the day, had so far increased, as to render him unable to stand up any longer. With great reluctance he

then went home, and at two þÿo clock, yesterday, (Sunday) died of Asiatic Cho- I þÿlera. þÿ ibid. To the Editor of the Colonial Standard and Jamaica Despatch. Sin, þÿ Science tells us þÿ When oxigen and nitrogen combine , they do not constitute air, but acid þÿpoisons. Who knows l ut this might be the main cause of Cholera. FRENCH OCCUPATION OF GREECE. A French expeditionary force arrived at the Pirseus on the night of the 25th inst. Immediately upon their arrival several merchant ships attempted to leave the harbour, but they were stopped by the French, time placed at the same and an embargo was upon all the vessels in port. The French also took possession, without loss of time, of three small Government vessels that were there, transferring the Greek sailors to their own ships, and allowing the Greek officers to go on shore. Next morning a large body of the French troops, some .'1,000, landed, and very quickly pitched their tents. No opposition was made to their landing ; and, in case of any, all the French steamers and a Prussian corvette stationed there had orders to fire. On the contrary, however, every assistance that could be rendered was rendered by the Greek gendarmerie. The French troops that were landed soon made themselves masters of the powder magazines and other military stores. Mons. From the Halifax Courin-, June 3, 1854. The Siege of Silistria. þÿ On the 16th Prince Paskiewitseh gave orders that the bombardment of Silistria should cease. We do not know whether this is to be attributed to the menacing attitude of Austria or to some negotiations for a capitulation that may be going on between the Russians and Turks. From subsequent announcements it appears that the siege operations had been resumed for a despatch from Bucharest, of the 22nd instant, announces that by news received direct from Kalarash, where the staff of Prince Paskiewitsch is at present, an outwork of the fortress of Silistria has been stormed and taken by the Russian army. The Turks after this sent a flag of truce to the Prince. Accounts from the neighbourhood ot Silistria received in Vienna represent that the Russians, after their partial success before that fortress, on the 21st inst., were repulsed by the Turks. According to information derived alike from both camps, it is certain that the Russians have suffered severely before Silistria. Some letters, and those not Turkish, carry their estimated loss to the enormous figure 8,000 men. The of traditional fame of the Ottomans as defenders of fortresses diminishes somewhat the apparent exaggeration of these numbers. The best artillerists of either camp are engaged in the attack and defence of this fortress. General Schilders is at the head of the entire artillery corps of the Russians, and Prince Gortschakoff belongs to the same arm of the

service. Mussa Pacha, the commandant (,f Silistria, is known as a scientific officer of artillery, and he has for coadjutors some of the Prussian artillery instructors, who have renounced their own nationality to make common cause with the Turks. For a time the Russians believed that they were certain to triumph, and obtain Silistria by gold, if not by arms, but a better knowledge of the character of Mussa has satisfied them that if they would take the fortress it must be as they took Ismail. Accord ing to the last accounts, Prince Paskic witsch had returned on the 22nd to Ka larasch, which he had quitted for the south bank on the LStli. The storming column was completely annihilated, and the Turks counted 1,500 Russian corps es, which were cast with some quicklime into a large pit. PROCEEDINGS OF THE COLONIAL COUNCIL Second Session The Citli meeting of the Council was held on Tuesday the 27th .Tune at II þÿo clock Absent were Messrs. ITeilbiitb, þÿMc Cutehin and Riise. The draft of a law on the introduction of new coins was explained by the mover Mr. Birch, and recommended to the attention of the Council by the Governor. After a short discussion the case was referred to a Committee of 5 members, to which were elected Messrs : Petersen with 13, Hanschell with 12, Birch with 1 1 , Ohsten with 9, Hawley with 9 votes. The accounts for St. Thomas and St. Johns Land Treasuries for the year 1851 having been given in by the ltevisors, elected last session, it was submitted to the resolution of the Council, in what manner the proposals drawn up by the Revisors for the decision of theso accounts should be treated, in order that the final decision thereon may be passed by the Council ; it was preliminarily resolved to refer the matter to a Committee, to which were elected Messrs : Hanschell with 12, Petersen with 10, Ohsten with 8 votes. The Council then entered upon the 1st discussion of the following 5 private Bills presented by Mr. DeGout. 1 ) A Bill proposing that the Council render a Testimonial of respect to the memory of the late Reverend Hanschell in consequence of the zeal and activity evinced by him as its member The Governor pointed out, that such manifestations could not be supposed to fall within the þÿCouncil sphere s of action, as a deliberative assembly, the task of which was to pass opinions
on matters belonging to the legislation for the Colonies Mr Hawley observed, that it was customary in other deliberative assemblies to express their

regret in the form of addresses to the family of the deceased at the loss of meritorious members, and on the strength of his personal acquaintance with the said member commented upon his just claim to such a testimonial. The Council adopted the suggestion of Mr. Arnesen, that a declaration be inserted in the protocol, that the Council availed itself of the opportunity offered by the proposition of Mr DeGout to declare that it regrets the loss of the late Reverend Hanschell as a valuable member of this community and of the Colonial Council. The Council then proceeded to the order of the day. 2) A Bill proposing the abolition of certain disqualifications supposed to establish differences between the rights of Danish subjects iu these Colonies, especially with regard to the right of naturalisation. The Governor having explained that the proposition partly regarded matters that were already decided by law, and partly arose from misconstruction, the mover withdrew the bill. 3) A Bill proposing that the Council be furnished with elucidations regarding the application of the fund for the education of Teachers. The Governor stated, that the interest of this fund had þÿ by the competent authorities, and after having duly obtained the sanction of the plurality of those by whose subscriptions it had been raised in the year 1828, þÿ been applied for the benefit of the schools throughout the ColoDy, and that it was not feasible now to make any alteration in this matter, which has been long

ago settled by the respective parties. The matter was in accordance with the proposition of Mr. Arnesen referred to the Government, the Governor having previously declared his willingness to receive it. 4) A Bill proposing the establishment of a new burial-ground in St. Thomas, i-c. The Governor expressed the desire, that the mover would in this quite local matter confer witli him personally, which was acceded to and the bill withdrawn. 5) A Bill regarding the eventual pensions to officers in case of reduction. The Governor observed, that there was no occasion at present to enter on this matter, and it being subsequently þÿ according to the lltli of the rules for business þÿ put to the vote if the bill should be accepted or not ; the case was rejected by the Council. The Chairman closed the meeting at 31 þÿo clock

The provisional ordinance of þÿ 26th March 1849, which in its 1st annuls the ordinance of 6th Juno 1833 and earlier ordinances respecting Commerce fic , fixes likewise fine, payment of duties and confiscation of goods when smuggled Hut the Royal provisional ordinance of 1st of goods when smuggled, without saying anything July 1849, which is emanated instead of the last mentioned provisional ordinance of 26th March 1849, stipulates in its 14th , Confiscation only about fine or duties, which Confiscation only is likewise stipulated in the lfith of the royal ordinance of 30th June 1850 the 16th of which royal ordinance repeals all prior ordinances regarding trade and navigation at St. Croix. Sir, þÿ In your just criticism on the changes which have lately heen made in the great offices of State there is one point on which þÿ more strongly I mean l lie disregard 1 wisli you had insisted which lias heen shown in the whole affair to the interests of the colonies. Among the reforms to which the present Ministry was virtually pledged not the least important was reform in our system of colonial government. Mr. Gladstone, the Duke of Newcastle, and Sir W. Molesworth had publicly professed the most advanced views on colonial reform, and the assumption of the Colo iiial-ortice by the Duke was regarded by the colonies as an earnest that those views were paramount in the Administration. 1 will not say that the. expec t;it ions thus formed have been realized. The Duke of Newcastle has governed 1 lie colonies liberally enough, it is true; hut lie lias done nothing towards the reform of the system of government under which they suffer, and which lie lias so often condemned. Still, up to this time the colonists have always hoped. They hud great confidence in the Duke's character, in his knowledge of colonial affairs, and in the deep interest lie was known to take in them. almost studiously avoided the subject ot colonial politics. From the St. Lucia Palladium , June 24. Cholera in Barbados and Grenada. We take this opportunity of presenting our unqualified thanks to our Barbados Correspondent lor his unremitting attention in forwarding to us from time to time statements of the progress of Cholera in that Island. In the present instance we are enabled to lay before our readers a complete tabular account from the commencement of the disease to the afternoon of the 19th inst. It will be seen that neither age, sex, condition nor colour has been spared. The rich man with all the comforts of civilized society and with all the care and attention which money could purchase, becomes equally with the squalid poor, a victim to the fell destroyer. Nearly one-eleventh of the inhabitants of the densely populated city of Bridgetown has been carried off since the commencement of this terrible scourge ; the Gaol has been swept with a worse than hurricane blast. The Military decimated ; the Police Force and the Shipping have furnished their victims; Government House has been invaded, and even those whose unhinged minds rendered them objects of charitable provision, have been hurried from their ideal world to that þÿ Bourne from . which there is no returning. The 8th Meeting of the Council was held Friday the 30th Juno at 11 þÿo clock. Under the 1st discussion of the draft of Law regarding the reorganisation of the Upper Court, the Chairman transferred his functions to the Vice Chairman, and the discussion was opened by the Speaker þÿ Birch, who explained, that the majority of the Committee, with the exception of an amendment of minor consequence, had agreed to the draft of Government ; but its member Petersen declared, that he could not deviate from his views of the case contained in his dissenting vote, dissuading the draft. The Council then entered upon tin discussion of the following 3 private bills from Mr. he Gout : 1) Proposing the establishment of a Gaol in St. Thomas. According to the proposal of Mr. Arnesen, this bill was referred to the combined Committee elected to report on the drafts relative to the assessment of sundry Taxes and Extra Taxes for the benefit of the Land Treasury of St. Thomas. 2) Proposing certain improvements to be effected in the Harbor of St. Thomas. Which Bill the mover requested to be referred to the Government. The Governor having observed, that the object of this bill, that of blasting some rocks in the harbor of St. Thomas, had already long time ago been the subject of þÿGovernment consideration, s and Mr. Castonier stating, that lie bad privately tried to blast the rocks in question, which he thought may be easily removed they being only formations of coral, the mover withdrew the motion.

3) Proposing that the Council be furnished with elucidations of the result of divers private bills, which were produced during the former session, and referred by the Council to the (iovernment. In consequence hereof the Governor explained the difference between a ease being discussed in Council and then accompanied with Council's opinion referred to the Government, and when it is merely referred to Government for its decision, in which latter case it must be considered as re jected by the Council, and its final decision, like other matters, left to Government The matters thus referred to Government are a, Bill regarding the establishment of a Board of Commerce iu St. Thomas. For the investigation of which the Government had on the 19tli February 1853 appointed a Committee, whose ultimate report in which a variety of opinions prevailed, had not been rendered before the 14th April þÿ1854 , and which would be laid before H. M. the King by the Ministry.

b, Bill recommending a more effectual system for the collection of the House Tax 4c. Regarding which the Gov. observed, that this had not been feasible on account of the existing laws. c, Bill recommending remuneration to be granted to several inhabitants in the town of Frederiksted or their estates, in consequence of losses sustained duriug the revolt on the 3d July 1848. The þÿMinistry s decision on this matter had already been communicated to the parties concerned. Finally the Governor notified, that he bad agreed upon with the Chairman, that those representations that the Colonial Council may, in accordance with the 1st section in the 5th of the Colonial Law and the Rules of Business, find occasion to make to the Governor, will ia future be inserted in the þÿCouncil s Proceedings, and that in such cases the þÿGovernor reply s thereto would be imparted to the Council after the opening of its next session ; but that this rule should not be applicable to such cases, where matters, conformably to the 2nd section of the said 5 had been referred to Government. The mover of these bills having stated his opinion regarding the elucidations given, which he did not consider satisfactory, the question was put to the vote, and a majority of 16 votes against I decided, that the matter should rest. The Governor declared the session of the Council prolonged for the succeeding two weeks, the legal term having expired. The Chairman closed the meeting at 3 þÿo clock.

From the Barbados Globe, June 22, 1854. Intelligence reached Town onMonday evening last that the greatest excitement and alarm had been occasioned in the parishes of St. James and St. Thomas

a v © ui % 2 a by the lawless and outrageous proceedings of a gang of laborers, who had gone into several estates, forcibly entered the premises and carried off whatever in the way of provision they could lay hands upon; that the greatest violence marked their proceedings, and the most alarming consequences to person and property were to be apprehended in the further progress of their marauding enterprise. A large body of the Police Force, mounted and armed, were promptly despatched to the aid of the local authorities, and a party of 50 men of the 3(5th Regiment simultaneously marched to Hole Town under command of Captain Rainsford, accompanied by Lieut. Lloyd and Staff' Surgeon Dr. Ross ; but on the arrival of these forces, the whole gang had disappeared and all was quiet. The ringleaders in this affair have been apprehended and are in prison. The West Indian gives the following particulars: þÿ We learn from a reliable source the following particulars of these outrages, which we hope will he effectually stopped by the energetic measures that were taken on the spot by the Police Magistrates of St. Thomas and St. James, and by the resident proprietors and managers. A mob of people began their depredations, and to show a disposition to violence and plunder at Turners Hall Estate in St. þÿAndrew where s upon a Hogshead of sugar which had been left on the top of the hill to be taken on to the Hole Town. They took out the sugar, and rolled the cask down a ravine. They then proceeded to Apes'

Hill and the Spring Estates where they forced open the Boiling Houses, and carried þÿoff a good deal of sugar. They then went over to Farmers across the gully, where they were reported by the Manager to he from 3 to 400 in number. They were here joined by several of the people on the Estate, and one of these named Griffith is said to have led the way into the provision house where they got hold of some 2000 weight of Yams. The Overseer Mr. McClean endeavoured to resist them, and was beaten in the scuffle, and was obliged to submit to all their demands, which however were i limited to such articles of food as were to he found on the Estate. They then proceeded on to Hilloby where the same scene was enacted ; and afterwards to Plumtree, where they broke into the Boiling House. Their numbers however were diminished to about J50 or 160. From Plumtree they came down to Flowers ; as they entered the Estate the Manager rang the bell, and called all the laborers into the yard, and urged them to defend the property of Mr. Daniel the

laborers from the neighbouring Estate j (lily manifested. þÿ Ilidgeway, and a fight ensued between the two parties; in which the pillagers got the worst of it, or seeing that they would get the worst of it, they quietly moved over the gullev to Lancaster and Westmoreland, at which last they found Mr. W. Manning, the Proprietor, who very coolly asked them their business ; and upon their saying they had come to get something to cat, said that lie would give them all the provision on the Estate, which was a few eddoes, and a pint of molasses each. They were content to receive this and afterwards dispersed. We learn that 20 of the ringleaders, 16 men and 4 women were apprehended, several of them at Blenoers. Amongst them, a whiteman named Dean, a tenant on Apes' Hill, who was said to have excited the negroes to these acts, and in whose house quantities of.sugar, molasses, yams, &. c., part of the plunder, were found. Griffith also, from Farmers is in custody- The Magistrates swore in Special Constables to aid the Police in restoring peace and capturing the rioters.

The sons of Mr. Armstrong at Fortress , were amongst the most active, and some men from Blowers. As soon as these outrages were made known to the Governor, he gave directions for the swearing in of these Constables, and to send the prisoners convicted of joining in them, the men to District A and C Station Houses, and the women to E. þÿ(Speights ). A company of gentlemen from Town also armed themselves, and went through the Estates in the eveeverything perfectly ning, hut found the roads deserted, a and quiet ; also detachment of the 36th Regiment, under Captain Rainsford, consisting of 40 men, was ordered to the Hole Town, where they remained during the night in the Wesleyan Chapel and the Station House ; and this morning returned about II þÿo clock, finding not the slightest appearance of insubordination, or attempt at pillage.

We are very happy to learn that, although the Epidemic is still distressingly prevalent in the city, there lias been a decided falling off' in the mortality since Sunday, and that there is every reason to believe it is abating in Town. Whilst, as we stated on Monday, the number of interments at Indian River on Saturday was 230, and on Sunday they seized 223, on Monday it fell down to 182, more than one half of which were from the rural district of the parish. On Tuesday, the interments þÿw ere186, yesterday 183 or thereabouts, and to-day 167, but many bodies brought from the rural district enter into these numbers. In the cing parishes, however, the disease lament with Giant strides we is advan- to state. From the paucity of Medical men as compared with the demands upon them just now, and the exertions which, as a natural consequence, private individuals and laymen are compelled to put forth, it is scarcely possible to get a line from friends in the rural districts, so that we are without particular and authentic accounts as to the real extent of the mortality. General information is all that can he got, from which it appears however, that in St. Joseph and Christ Church, St. Thomas, St. Andrews, and St. Lucy, wherever there are large villages, the number of victims has been very great. In St. Joseph the deaths have been already nearly 200, and on one estate alone in St. Lucy 30 have been swept oft'. The Health Authorities in the respective parishes, zealously rein-

forced by private gentlemen, are, mean while, everywhere indefatigable in their exertions to modify the virulence of the Epidemic, and we trust the good effects proprietor. They were joined by the j of their combined efforts will he spec Ibid.

Mate of Colonial society, the abrogation of the disqualifications which establish an invidious distinction among the Danish Subjects, who acknowledge the same allegiance, claim the same right, are liable to the same duties and responsibilities, nevertheless some partially protected, and others restricted by exceptional 2nd Session. 6th Sitting. The progress and welfare of society, in the Danish Colonies, are exposed to obstacles which it is in the power, and 1 believe the desire of the Government to remove, when impartially represented ; these exigencies now present themselves, owing to the great incon- /enience and anxiety ot the parties, resident subjects, either natives or Burghers permanently settled in these Islands. The evil originates in the imperfect state of the ordinances in operation in these Islandsþÿ remnants of the Laws of Denmark and those mutilated. The question has been frequently, and publicly discussed in the mother country, in regard to the expediency of extend mg to the Colonies the Fundamental Law or extracts therefrom. The existence of the Colonial Council offer the medium, to obtain, by a fair representation to His M. Government, the attention necessary to remedy the grievous position of the inhabitants : the absence of such þÿ þÿCode is an anomaly, in as much, that on a compre-

hensive view of the state of the Colonies, no reasonable objection can be adduced to retard the legislative enactments which are necessary to the wellbeing of the people. The Case of CaptainJ. A. Kjxk. The Father of this individual was born in the country of Tliisted in Jutland, Denmark, and the subject of this sketch was born in Norway in the year 1795, consequently under the Danish Government. Capt. K j a: k went to sea at 10 years, as the war soon followed, he was old enough for public service. On the 15th October 1811 by a special Patent from the Admiralty in Copenhagen, he was appointed to the station of apprentice þÿ Volunteur þÿPatent until qualified and appointed ship Master. Being on that station since 1812 he received, at the same time, the permission to sail in that capacity in the provision trade, between Norway and Denmark, being too young to be entitled to Burghers Brief. In the following year he remained principally in Denmark, until the spring of 1819 consequently one year before the period of six years havi.ig expired, as stipulated in the 20th Article of the Treaty of Peace, dated January 14th 1814. On the 6th July 1820, ho presented a memorial to the high Court of Chancery (Cancellict) for naturalization and per-

mission to be received as a Burgher in Copenhagen as well as shipmaster. from the Admiralty to remain in St. Thomas as Harbour master assistant. þÿ The ship returning to Europe ; though in good health up to this period, a dangerous attack of fever compelled him to undertake a voyage for the benefit of his health as a ship master from the Port of St. Thomas. On the 24th Sept. 1828 Capt. Kj;er was appointed assistant to the Captain of the Port, and at different periods, forming a lapse of about ten years, remained as Harbour master by the sanction of the Government. On the announcement that the Harbour þÿMaster s situation would become vacant on the 1st ApTil, owing to the retirement of Commodore Rhode on a pension, Capt. This course was not adopted owing to the information received by a letter from the Finance Department, dated 4th April, in which it is stated, that the said Department had entered into a correspondence with the Minister of Justice, and the Minister of Home Department, and the result was, that Capt. A Bill submitting to the Council various documents connected with the administration of General von Scholten and the Burgher Council of 1829, relative to the project of commemorating the Nuptials of their Royal Highnesses the Princess Wilhelinino Maria and Prince Frederick Carl Christian, by raisiug a fund for the educating of Teachers to be eraployod in the Schools in the Danish West India Islands. 2nd Session. 6th Sitting. The documents which refer to the collecting of a fund for the purpose of educating Teachers for the Schools of the Danish West India Islands indicate the extent of progress made at the time, by the projectors, in the accumulating by sub-

scription the funds necessary to accomplish the benevolent object ; notwithstanding these advantages, no practical operation appears of the performance ol the task which devolved on the par- ties entrusted with the management ' The subject matter being one of peculiar interest, the Case is hereby submitted to the consideration of the Council, for the purpose of obtaining the elucidations which the Government may be disposed to offer, either as to the regular appropriation of the fund, or contrary to the original purpose. The following statement is respectfully submitted without the presumption to ensure its accuracy, but merely, as indications likely to forward the investigation of the subject. It appears, that the Capital ol the fund for the educating of Teachers for the Schools in the Danish West India Islands, amounting to Ps. 1 1,278 90 or $ 7,218 52 was invested in the Estate Oxford on the 29th May 1841, subject to the interest of 6 per cent.
